items.lessonTitle: the tattoo that's really about today

neighbors.heading: the greatest wonder
neighbors.text: Today Marcus told himself: death is near, so be good while you can. The Mahabharata asks it as a riddle. A spirit at a lake asks Yudhishthira: what is the greatest wonder? He answers, in paraphrase: every day, creatures go to death, and still the living act as if they will live forever.
neighbors.difference: Marcus writes as a Stoic reminding himself to act well. In the epic, the answer comes inside a teaching where the true self is not born and does not die; what ends is one body, one life.
neighbors.shared: remembering the end can wake you up to today.
neighbors.sources: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, the Yaksha's questions (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: one day before
neighbors.text: Today the end came into view, so the middle could come clear. The rabbis have a teaching like that. Rabbi Eliezer said: return to God one day before your death. His students asked, how can anyone know that day? Then return today, he said, since tomorrow you might die, and your whole life will be spent returning.
neighbors.difference: Marcus aims at being good by reason and nature. Rabbi Eliezer's word is teshuvah, turning back to God and the commandments, a return the Jewish year also sets aside days for.
neighbors.shared: don't save the good you mean to do for later.

items.lessonTitle: the Tao: those who know they have enough are rich

neighbors.heading: learning content
neighbors.text: Today the Tao Te Ching said knowing enough is what rich is. Paul says something close, in a letter to friends in Philippi: "I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content." Learned, he says. Not born with it. He goes on that he knows how to have little and how to have plenty.
neighbors.difference: The Tao Te Ching finds enough by knowing your own lot. Paul ties his contentment to Christ: "I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me."
neighbors.shared: enough is something you can learn, a little at a time.

neighbors.heading: riches of the soul
neighbors.text: Today an old saying taught that knowing enough is the real wealth. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said it in his own way: riches are not in having many things; real riches are the richness of the soul. Muslims often call this contentment qana'ah, being satisfied with what God has given.
neighbors.difference: Lao-tzu's saying is about knowing yourself and the Way. For Muslims, contentment rests on trust in God as the provider, and it sits beside giving: a share of wealth is owed to others as zakat.
neighbors.shared: the richest heart is the one that can say "enough."

items.lessonTitle: the rule that keeps turning up

neighbors.heading: a father's advice
neighbors.text: Today the rule turned up in China, in Hillel, in Jesus. Catholic Bibles hold another version, in the book of Tobias. A father, thinking he may die soon, gives his son advice for life: "See thou never do to another what thou wouldst hate to have done to thee by another."
neighbors.difference: Confucius gives the rule as one word to live by. For Catholics, it sits in Scripture, and the Church reads it as part of the law written on the heart, fulfilled in Christ's command to love.
neighbors.shared: your own heart can be a map of someone else's.
neighbors.sources: Tobias 4:16 (Douay-Rheims; Tobit 4:15 in many Bibles) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 1789 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: no one is a stranger
neighbors.text: Today the golden rule asked you to read someone else's heart through your own. Guru Arjan Dev, the fifth Sikh Guru, sings of where that can lead. In a hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib he says, in paraphrase: no one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger; I get along with everyone.
neighbors.difference: The golden rule is a rule for how to act. The Guru speaks of a changed heart, given through the company of the holy and the Guru's grace, that sees God in everyone.
neighbors.shared: the people around you are not strangers.

items.lessonTitle: Marcus doesn't want to get up

neighbors.heading: strong as a lion
neighbors.text: Today an emperor argued with his pillow. A classic code of Jewish law begins right there, at the edge of the bed. The Shulchan Aruch opens, in paraphrase: be strong as a lion to get up in the morning to serve your Creator. Many Jews then say a short thanks on waking, Modeh Ani, before the day begins.
neighbors.difference: Marcus rises to a human's work because nature made him for it. In Jewish law, the morning is for serving God, and the day that follows is shaped by the commandments.
neighbors.shared: getting up can be the first good thing you do.
neighbors.sources: Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chayim 1:1 (paraphrase) · Modeh Ani (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: rouse yourself
neighbors.text: Today Marcus haggled with his blankets and won. The Dhammapada has a verse for that hour: "He who does not rouse himself when it is time to rise, who, though young and strong, is full of sloth... that lazy and idle man will never find the way to knowledge."
neighbors.difference: Marcus gets up to do his part in a world ordered by reason. In the Dhammapada, rising is effort on the path to wisdom and freedom from suffering.
neighbors.shared: the morning asks for one small, brave yes.

neighbors.heading: a traveler on the road
neighbors.text: Today Diogenes threw away his cup because a child drank from his hands. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ once took a young companion by the shoulder and told him, in paraphrase: be in this world as if you were a stranger, or someone passing through on the road. A traveler carries what the journey needs.
neighbors.difference: Diogenes chose to own almost nothing, to be free. Islam doesn't ask most people to give up their things; it asks them to hold them lightly, give in charity, and remember the journey leads back to God.
neighbors.shared: carry lightly; you're only passing through.

neighbors.heading: enjoy by letting go
neighbors.text: Today a cup went into the dirt and a man felt freer. The Isha Upanishad opens with a verse many Hindus know well. In paraphrase: everything that moves in this world is dwelt in by the Lord. Enjoy it by letting it go. Don't covet anyone's wealth.
neighbors.difference: Diogenes put things down to be free of them. The Upanishad doesn't ask you to throw them away; it asks you to see everything as God's, and so to hold it without grasping.
neighbors.shared: open hands can hold the most.

neighbors.heading: everyone sits in one row
neighbors.text: Today a fur coat got the soup and the person went hungry. Sikhs built an answer into the gurdwara: langar, the free kitchen. Everyone sits on the floor together, side by side in rows, and eats the same simple meal. Tradition says Guru Amar Das asked even an emperor to sit and eat in the row before meeting him.
neighbors.difference: Nasruddin shows the problem with a joke. Langar answers it with a shared meal, offered as service to God and to everyone who comes, whatever their faith or their clothes.
neighbors.shared: at the best tables, nobody checks your coat.
neighbors.sources: Langar, the Sikh community kitchen (paraphrase) · Guru Amar Das and Emperor Akbar (tradition)

neighbors.heading: who to invite
neighbors.text: Today Nasruddin let a coat eat at a banquet. Jesus, at a dinner of his own, told his host who belongs at the table: "But when thou makest a feast, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind: And thou shalt be blessed; for they cannot recompense thee."
neighbors.difference: Nasruddin's joke holds up a mirror. Jesus gives an invitation list, and promises the host a reward "at the resurrection of the just," from God, not from the guests.
neighbors.shared: the guest who can't pay you back is the one to call.

neighbors.heading: knowing while you eat
neighbors.text: Today Zhaozhou sent a new monk back to his bowl. That's a Zen story, and the Buddha's older teachings in the Pali texts say it plainly too. In the discourse on the foundations of mindfulness, a monk is taught to act with clear knowing while eating, drinking, chewing and tasting, and even while walking or getting dressed.
neighbors.difference: Zen teaches it in a sudden exchange a student has to wake up to. The Pali suttas lay it out step by step, as a practice trained over time.
neighbors.shared: the plainest moment can be the whole practice.

neighbors.heading: vessels of the altar
neighbors.text: Today the teaching was in a bowl and warm water. Saint Benedict wrote a rule for monks that still guides monasteries. About the monk who keeps the kitchen and stores, he says, in paraphrase: let him treat every pot and tool of the monastery as if it were one of the holy vessels of the altar.
neighbors.difference: For Zhaozhou, the bowl is the practice, nothing added. For Benedict, ordinary work is holy because it's done for God, in a life of prayer and work together.
neighbors.shared: there are no small dishes.

neighbors.heading: worn-out clothes
neighbors.text: Today Zhuangzi grieved, then saw his wife's life as one more turn of the seasons. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna comforts a grieving Arjuna with a picture. In paraphrase: as a person throws off worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, the self leaves worn-out bodies and takes on new ones.
neighbors.difference: Zhuangzi sees life and death as change in the great flow of things, and doesn't say what goes on. The Gita teaches a self that is never born and never dies, moving from body to body.
neighbors.shared: a loss can be held inside something larger, still moving.

neighbors.heading: a time to mourn
neighbors.text: Today Zhuangzi heard the year turning in his grief. Ecclesiastes knows the seasons too: "A time to be born, and a time to die... A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance." Jewish mourners sit shiva for a week, and the community comes to them.
neighbors.difference: Zhuangzi drummed soon after his first grief. Jewish tradition gives mourning its own set days, and mourners say Kaddish, a prayer praising God, for months.
neighbors.shared: grief belongs to the turning of the year.
neighbors.sources: Ecclesiastes 3:2, 3:4 (JPS 1917) · shiva and the Mourner's Kaddish (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: one plants, one waters
neighbors.text: Today an old man planted a tree he would never eat from. Paul wrote to a church arguing over which teacher mattered most. His answer is a garden: "I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase." Each did a part. Neither did it all.
neighbors.difference: The Talmud's old man plants for his grandchildren, as his ancestors planted for him. Paul speaks of planting faith in a church, and gives the growing to God.
neighbors.shared: you can plant shade you'll never sit in.

neighbors.heading: plant it anyway
neighbors.text: Today a carob tree took seventy years to bear fruit. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ went further. He said, in paraphrase: if the Last Hour comes while one of you holds a palm seedling in his hand, and he can plant it before it comes, let him plant it.
neighbors.difference: Honi's old man plants for the people after him. In the hadith, there may be no one after, and the planting is still worth doing, as a good deed before God.
neighbors.shared: plant the good thing, whoever eats the fruit.

items.lessonTitle: The north wind and the sun

neighbors.heading: a mild answer
neighbors.text: Today the sun won the cloak without touching the traveler. Catholic Bibles keep the same wisdom in Proverbs: "A mild answer breaketh wrath: but a harsh word stirreth up fury." Saint Francis de Sales, a bishop known for his gentleness, is remembered for saying more flies are caught with a spoonful of honey than a barrel of vinegar.
neighbors.difference: Aesop's fable is practical advice about persuasion. For Catholics, gentleness is a virtue, a fruit of the Holy Spirit, practiced out of love more than to win.
neighbors.shared: warmth opens what force only closes.
neighbors.sources: Proverbs 15:1 (Douay-Rheims) · Galatians 5:23 · Francis de Sales, attributed (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: answer evil with good
neighbors.text: Today the north wind blew and the traveler only held on tighter. Baba Farid, a Sufi saint whose verses are kept in the Guru Granth Sahib, says, in paraphrase: answer evil with goodness, and don't fill your mind with anger. Guru Nanak praises sweetness and humility as the heart of virtue.
neighbors.difference: The fable is about changing someone else's mind. Farid's verse is about keeping your own heart clean before God, whether or not the other person ever changes.
neighbors.shared: a gentle answer leaves both people warmer.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1381-1382, sloks of Farid; Ang 470, Asa di Var (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: not for the reward
neighbors.text: Today Rabia carried fire and water so love would have no bargain left in it. Long before her, the rabbis kept a saying of Antigonus of Sokho. In paraphrase: don't be like servants who serve their master to get a reward. Be like servants who serve with no thought of reward, and let the awe of Heaven be upon you.
neighbors.difference: Rabia's love for God is the Sufi path of longing, told in stories. Antigonus speaks of serving God through the commandments, and pairs that service with awe.
neighbors.shared: some love doesn't need a receipt.

neighbors.heading: the heartwood
neighbors.text: Today Rabia asked what's left when the reward is gone. The Buddha told of a man who needs heartwood, the strong core of a tree, but walks off with twigs or bark. So too, he said, is someone who takes up the path and settles for gain, praise or fame, and misses its heart: a mind truly free.
neighbors.difference: Rabia's love is for God alone. The Buddha points not to a God but to the freedom of the mind itself as the core of the path.
neighbors.shared: don't stop at the bark; go for the heart.

neighbors.heading: the lost camel
neighbors.text: Today a father ran down the road to a son coming home. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told of a man in the desert who lost his camel, with his food and water on it, then found it standing beside him again. God, he said, is more glad at a servant's turning back than that man was.
neighbors.difference: Christians read the father in Jesus's parable as a picture of God's welcome in Christ. In Islam, the one who repents turns straight to God, with no one in between.
neighbors.shared: the way home is open before you finish your apology.

neighbors.heading: soon made right
neighbors.text: Today the son rehearsed his speech and never got to finish it. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says, in paraphrase: even if someone has done great wrong, if they turn to me with their whole heart, count them as good, for they have chosen rightly. Soon they become righteous and find lasting peace.
neighbors.difference: In Luke, the son comes home to his father's house. In the Gita, the turning is devotion, bhakti, to Krishna, and it reshapes the person from within.
neighbors.shared: no one has walked too far to turn around.

items.lessonTitle: I know that I don't know

neighbors.heading: no one knows the end
neighbors.text: Today Socrates found he was wise only in knowing what he didn't know. Guru Nanak sings something close in Japji, at the opening of the Guru Granth Sahib. In paraphrase: there is no end to praising God, no end to God's gifts. Many long to know the limit, and no one can find it. The more is said, the more remains.
neighbors.difference: Socrates questioned people to find the edge of human knowing. Guru Nanak stands before God, whose greatness has no edge, and answers with praise.
neighbors.shared: "i don't know" can be the start of wonder.
neighbors.sources: Japji Sahib, pauri 24, Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 5 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: as he ought to know
neighbors.text: Today Socrates found that thinking you know is the real trap. Paul warned a church proud of its knowledge: "And if any man think that he knoweth any thing, he knoweth nothing yet as he ought to know." In the next verse he points somewhere else: love.
neighbors.difference: Socrates kept questioning as the path to wisdom. Paul says knowledge alone puffs up, and that loving God, and being known by him, matters more than knowing.
neighbors.shared: humble learners are the ones who keep learning.

neighbors.heading: check it against the texts
neighbors.text: Today you heard why every story here has an address. The Buddha, near the end of his life, told his monks what to do when someone claims, I heard this from the Buddha himself. In paraphrase: don't accept it, and don't reject it. Check it against the teachings and the discipline. If it fits, keep it. If not, set it aside.
neighbors.difference: This path names sources out of honesty and thanks. For Buddhists, checking is how the Buddha's own teaching is kept true after him.
neighbors.shared: a teaching worth keeping is worth tracing home.
neighbors.sources: Digha Nikaya 16, Mahaparinibbana Sutta, the four great references (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: what I also received
neighbors.text: Today a teaching with no address couldn't be visited. Paul gives his: "For I delivered unto you first of all, which I also received." Catholics speak of tradition this way, a faith handed down from the apostles through the Church, generation to generation.
neighbors.difference: This path keeps sources so readers can go back and check. For Catholics, the handing down itself is guided by the Holy Spirit, and the Church guards and teaches it.
neighbors.shared: what we know came to us through someone's hands.
neighbors.sources: 1 Corinthians 15:3 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 75-78 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: no ill will to anyone
neighbors.text: Today Marcus decided at dawn that difficult people are his kin. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna describes the person dear to him. In paraphrase: one who bears ill will to no being, who is friendly and compassionate, free of ego, steady in pleasure and pain, and forgiving.
neighbors.difference: Marcus reasons it out: we share one nature, made to work together. The Gita draws it from devotion, a heart given to God that sees God in every being.
neighbors.shared: decide before the day starts how you'll meet people.

neighbors.heading: before the morning prayers
neighbors.text: Today Marcus packed his patience before leaving the house. Many Jewish prayer books have a line to say before the morning prayers, a custom from the mystic Isaac Luria. In paraphrase: I take upon myself the commandment, love your neighbor as yourself. Some say it every morning, before they begin to pray.
neighbors.difference: Marcus prepares by reminding himself people don't know better. The Jewish line takes on a commandment from the Torah, so that loving others comes first, even before prayer.
neighbors.shared: start the day already on everyone's side.
neighbors.sources: Leviticus 19:18 · morning custom of Isaac Luria, in many siddurim (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the horse is prepared
neighbors.text: Today the archer did everything well, then let the arrow go. Proverbs puts it in a soldier's picture: "The horse is prepared against the day of battle: but safety is of the LORD." Getting the horse ready is yours. The outcome is in other hands.
neighbors.difference: Cato's Stoic moves the scoreboard to the shot itself. Proverbs places the outcome in God's hands, and many Christians pray over the work they've done.
neighbors.shared: do your part fully, then open your hand.

neighbors.heading: tie your camel
neighbors.text: Today Cato's archer aimed, then let go. A man once asked the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ whether he should tie up his camel or leave it loose and trust God. The answer, in paraphrase: tie it, and trust God. Muslims call this trust tawakkul.
neighbors.difference: For the Stoic, the arrow's flight belongs to chance and nature. For Muslims, what happens after you've done your part is in God's care, and trusting him is part of faith.
neighbors.shared: prepare well, then let the rest go.

neighbors.heading: never forget
neighbors.text: Today a study put the grandmother's advice to the test. Catholics pray the same advice in a psalm: "Bless the Lord, O my soul, and never forget all he hath done for thee." Then the psalm starts counting: who forgiveth, who healeth, who redeemeth, who crowneth thee with mercy.
neighbors.difference: The study counts blessings to notice them. The psalm counts them to thank Someone, and Catholics pray it in the Church's daily prayer.
neighbors.shared: what you count is what you come to see.

neighbors.heading: the giver keeps giving
neighbors.text: Today you counted your blessings once a week. Guru Nanak, in Japji, the morning prayer, says, in paraphrase: the Giver keeps on giving, and those who receive grow tired of receiving. Age after age, we live on what is given.
neighbors.difference: Gratitude studies measure how counting changes us. The Guru turns the counting toward the one Giver, God, whose gifts outlast anyone's list.
neighbors.shared: there are always more gifts than we can count.
neighbors.sources: Japji Sahib, pauri 3, Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 2 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: one ancestor
neighbors.text: Today astronauts looked down and saw one world. The Mishnah asks why the Torah tells of humanity starting from one single person. One answer, in paraphrase: so that no one could say to another, my father is greater than yours. Everyone goes back to the same parent.
neighbors.difference: The overview effect came from a view from orbit. The Mishnah draws it from the story of creation, where every human is made in God's image.
neighbors.shared: one family, on one small home.

neighbors.heading: rivers in the ocean
neighbors.text: Today the borders vanished from orbit. The Buddha gave a picture for the same thing. When the great rivers reach the ocean, he said, they lose their old names and are simply called the ocean. In the same way, people from every caste who joined his community left the old labels behind.
neighbors.difference: Astronauts felt it as one planet. The Buddha spoke of a community on a path, where birth no longer sorted people.
neighbors.shared: from far enough away, the lines on the map disappear.

neighbors.heading: walk gently
neighbors.text: Today a monk walked twenty paces and back, with nowhere to arrive. The Qur'an describes how God's servants walk: "The (faithful) slaves of the Beneficent are they who walk upon the earth modestly, and when the foolish ones address them answer: Peace."
neighbors.difference: Walking meditation pays close attention to each step. The verse is about the spirit of the walk, humble before God and peaceful with others.
neighbors.shared: the way you walk can be a quiet kindness.

neighbors.heading: walking around
neighbors.text: Today every step was the whole trip. Many Hindus walk a loop around a temple's shrine, called pradakshina, slowly and clockwise, keeping God on their right. Some walk around a whole sacred hill or town. The walk isn't to get somewhere. It's a way to stay close.
neighbors.difference: Cankama walks a straight line to know the step itself. Pradakshina circles a center, an act of devotion with God in the middle.
neighbors.shared: a walk with nowhere to go can bring you home.

neighbors.heading: seva
neighbors.text: Today the walk home after helping felt lighter. Sikhs call service seva: cooking in the free kitchen, cleaning shoes at the gurdwara door, any work done for others with no reward in mind. Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase: serve in this world, and you'll find a place of honor in God's court.
neighbors.difference: Research looks at how helping changes the helper's mood. Sikhs hold that seva should be selfless, and that its gift is humility and nearness to God.
neighbors.shared: serving others has a way of lifting the server.

neighbors.heading: more blessed to give
neighbors.text: Today the helper went home better off. Paul, saying goodbye to friends from Ephesus, reminded them of words he passed on from Jesus: "It is more blessed to give than to receive." He said it after years of working with his own hands to help the weak.
neighbors.difference: The studies find a link, not a promise. For Christians, the blessing of giving comes from God, and helping is love for Christ in the person helped.
neighbors.shared: giving often hands something back.

neighbors.heading: the observance day
neighbors.text: Today you met Shabbat, a day off from making. Buddhists keep a day of their own, uposatha, on the moon days each month. Many lay people visit the monastery, listen to teaching, and take on extra precepts for a day and a night: simpler eating, no entertainment, quiet.
neighbors.difference: Shabbat is a commandment and a rest given by God, belonging to the Jewish people. Uposatha is a day of practice, set by the moon, for training the mind.
neighbors.shared: a day set apart keeps the rest from rushing.

neighbors.heading: the Lord's day
neighbors.text: Today the sabbath came on the seventh day. Catholics keep Sunday, the day of the Resurrection. The commandment says: "Remember that thou keep holy the sabbath day." The Church asks the faithful to go to Mass and to set aside work that gets in the way of worship, joy, rest and works of mercy.
neighbors.difference: The Jewish Sabbath is Saturday, kept with its own laws. Catholics keep Sunday, honoring Christ's rising, and fill it with Mass, family and rest.
neighbors.shared: once a week, the world can wait.
neighbors.sources: Exodus 20:8 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 2180-2185 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: your own path
neighbors.text: Today you chose five practices that fit your life, not someone else's. The Bhagavad Gita has a line on that. Krishna says, in paraphrase: better to follow your own dharma, even imperfectly, than someone else's dharma done well.
neighbors.difference: Choosing five practices is about what fits your days. In the Gita, svadharma is your own duty in life, set by who you are and where you stand.
neighbors.shared: a path fits best when it's truly yours.

neighbors.heading: make it fixed
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said a person who's everywhere is nowhere. The rabbi Shammai gave a three-part rule. In paraphrase: make your Torah study a fixed habit; say little and do much; greet everyone with a cheerful face.
neighbors.difference: Seneca and Gollwitzer help you pick and anchor a few practices. Shammai's fixed time is for Torah study, a commandment, not a chosen tool.
neighbors.shared: a little, kept steady, outlasts a lot done once.

neighbors.heading: seven times
neighbors.text: Today a missed day turned out to be just a missed day. Proverbs says it about falling: "For a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again." Notice who it calls just. Not the one who never falls. The one who keeps getting up.
neighbors.difference: The habit study talks about practices that grow automatic. Proverbs speaks of a life lived before God, where rising again is part of being righteous.
neighbors.shared: getting up again is the practice.

neighbors.heading: pray it when you remember
neighbors.text: Today the instruction was: just do today's practice, today. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ gave a plain rule for a prayer someone forgot or slept through. In paraphrase: pray it when you remember it. Nothing more is asked to make up for it.
neighbors.difference: A daily habit on this path is a personal choice. The five daily prayers are a duty Muslims owe to God, which is why a missed one is made up.
neighbors.shared: when you remember, begin again. no speech needed.

neighbors.heading: a restless heart
neighbors.text: Today a reed cut from its bed sang of wanting to go home. Saint Augustine opened his Confessions with the same ache, speaking to God: "for Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee."
neighbors.difference: Rumi's reed is a Sufi picture of the soul's longing to return. Augustine speaks to a personal God, and Catholics find that rest in Christ and his Church.
neighbors.shared: the longing itself can be a kind of music.

neighbors.heading: longing is the king
neighbors.text: Today the flute's song came from being cut away. Baba Farid's verses in the Guru Granth Sahib honor that ache. In paraphrase: people speak of the pain of separation, but separation is the king; a body that never feels this longing is like a cremation ground.
neighbors.difference: Rumi's reed longs for the reedbed. In Sikh scripture, the longing is for the one God, met through the Name and the Guru's word.
neighbors.shared: missing home is how you know you have one.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1379, sloks of Farid (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: As if it were the last

neighbors.heading: one day before
neighbors.text: Today Marcus said to do each act as if it were the last. The rabbis said it too. Rabbi Eliezer taught: repent one day before your death. His students asked how anyone knows that day. Then repent today, he said, so all your days are spent returning. The Talmud leans on a verse: "Let thy garments be always white."
neighbors.difference: Marcus wanted presence without pretense, and left open what comes after. For Jews, the urgency is teshuvah, turning back to God and to the people you've wronged, with God waiting to receive it.
neighbors.shared: you don't have to wait for a someday to begin again.
neighbors.sources: Pirkei Avot 2:10, 2:15 in some editions (paraphrase) · Talmud, Shabbat 153a (paraphrase) · Ecclesiastes 9:8 (JPS 1917)

neighbors.heading: with diligence
neighbors.text: Today Marcus said to live each act as if it were the last. Buddhists keep that thought close. The Buddha once praised the monk who thinks, may I live just one more breath, and give it all to practice. His last words, as Rhys Davids gives them: "Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!"
neighbors.difference: Marcus wrote as a Stoic, trusting reason and the gods. Buddhists remember death to loosen clinging and to walk toward awakening, with no creator behind it and with rebirth in view.
neighbors.shared: knowing time is short can make this moment whole.
neighbors.sources: Anguttara Nikaya 6.19, on mindfulness of death (paraphrase) · Mahaparinibbana Sutta, Digha Nikaya 16 (Rhys Davids)

neighbors.heading: don't wait for morning
neighbors.text: Today Marcus said the only life you ever lose is the one you're living now. Muslims know a saying close to it. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told Ibn Umar to be in this world like a stranger or a traveler. And Ibn Umar used to say: when evening comes, don't wait for morning; when morning comes, don't wait for evening.
neighbors.difference: For Marcus, the present is all anyone holds, whatever comes after. For Muslims, this life is a journey toward Allah and the life to come, so each moment is a trust to use well.
neighbors.shared: this moment is the one in your hands.

neighbors.heading: the act, not the fruit
neighbors.text: Today Marcus said the present is the only thing anyone has. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna points Arjuna to the same place. Your right is to the work in front of you, he says, never to its fruits. Don't let the result be your reason, and don't stop working either. The doing is here; the outcome isn't.
neighbors.difference: Marcus reasoned that past and future aren't ours to lose. Krishna's teaching is about duty and devotion, offering each act to God and letting the fruit go.
neighbors.shared: give yourself to what's in front of you, and let the rest come.

neighbors.heading: why search the forest?
neighbors.text: Today Marcus said you can retreat into your own mind at any hour. Sikhs hear a hymn of the ninth Guru, Guru Tegh Bahadur: why go searching in the forest? The Lord lives in everyone and is always with you, like fragrance in a flower, like a reflection in a mirror. Look within.
neighbors.difference: Marcus's retreat is a room of calm thoughts, his own reason. For Sikhs, what's found within is the Creator, met through remembering the Name, and a Sikh doesn't leave home and family to find it.
neighbors.shared: the quiet place you're looking for may already be inside you.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 684, Guru Tegh Bahadur (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: shut the door
neighbors.text: Today Marcus said there's no quieter place than your own mind. Jesus pointed to a quiet room too: "But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret." Some Christians keep a small inner room like that, even on a crowded day.
neighbors.difference: Marcus stepped inward to steady his own thoughts. For Christians, the inner room isn't empty; it's where they speak with God as a Father who sees in secret.
neighbors.shared: you can always step into a quiet room inside.

neighbors.heading: made of thoughts
neighbors.text: Today Marcus said the soul takes the color of its thoughts. The Dhammapada opens the same way, in Max Müller's words: "All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts." Buddhists train the mind gently, again and again, because the mind is what shapes a life.
neighbors.difference: Marcus wanted to dye his soul with good thoughts guided by reason. Buddhists see the mind as always changing, with no fixed soul underneath, and train it toward freedom from suffering.
neighbors.shared: what you keep thinking slowly becomes who you are.

neighbors.heading: think on these things
neighbors.text: Today Marcus said the mind is dyed by the thoughts it keeps. Saint Paul gave the early Christians at Philippi a list to keep: whatever is true, just, holy and lovely, whatever has virtue in it, "think on these things." Catholics still turn to his list, and to prayers like the rosary, to fill the mind with what is good.
neighbors.difference: Marcus chose his own thoughts by reason. For Catholics, a good mind isn't only self-made; it grows with God's grace, through prayer and the sacraments.
neighbors.shared: you can choose what you let your mind soak in.

neighbors.heading: known by not knowing
neighbors.text: Today Rumi's townspeople touched one part of the elephant and named the whole. The Kena Upanishad says something just as humbling. The highest is known by the one who doesn't claim to know it, and missed by those who are sure they've grasped it. It is beyond what eye and word and mind can reach.
neighbors.difference: Rumi was a Muslim poet whose candle is the eye of the heart, given by God. The Upanishad points to Brahman, the one reality, known as the self within, beyond any knowing that grasps.
neighbors.shared: what we touch is real, and the whole is still bigger.

neighbors.heading: higher than the heavens
neighbors.text: Today Rumi said our senses are a palm in the dark, touching only part. The prophet Isaiah says something like it: "For My thoughts are not your thoughts, Neither are your ways My ways, saith the LORD." As the heavens are higher than the earth, he goes on, so are God's ways higher than ours.
neighbors.difference: Rumi's answer is a candle, the eye of the heart, a different way of seeing. In Isaiah, the gap is between people and God, and the bridge is God's own word, not a new way of seeing.
neighbors.shared: it's good to remember how much is bigger than our hands.

neighbors.heading: no thought for the morrow
neighbors.text: Today Marcus said not to let the future trouble you, because you'll meet it with the same mind you have now. Jesus said something close in the Sermon on the Mount: "Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof."
neighbors.difference: Marcus trusts the reason you carry with you. Jesus asks his listeners to trust their heavenly Father, who feeds the birds and clothes the lilies.
neighbors.shared: tomorrow doesn't have to be carried today.

neighbors.heading: if Allah wills
neighbors.text: Today Marcus said you'll meet tomorrow with the same tools you have today. Muslims hand tomorrow over in a small phrase, in sha' Allah, if God wills. The Qur'an teaches it: "And say not of anything: Lo! I shall do that tomorrow, Except if Allah will." Make the plan, do the work, and let tomorrow rest with God.
neighbors.difference: Marcus relied on his own reason to meet what comes. For Muslims, tomorrow belongs to Allah, and peace comes from trusting him while still doing their part.
neighbors.shared: you can plan for tomorrow without carrying it all tonight.

neighbors.heading: the clean of heart
neighbors.text: Today Rumi's painters polished a wall until it shone like a mirror. Jesus spoke of a clear heart, too: "Blessed are the clean of heart: for they shall see God." Catholics speak of keeping the heart clean through prayer, confession and mercy, so there's room in it for God.
neighbors.difference: Rumi, a Muslim mystic, pictures the Sufi heart polished of greed and envy. For Catholics, a clean heart is a gift of God's grace, renewed in the sacraments, not only something we polish ourselves.
neighbors.shared: a clear heart can take in more than a full one.

neighbors.heading: washed by the Name
neighbors.text: Today Rumi said the heart's work is clearing away, not adding more. Many Sikhs recite something like it each morning in the Japji. When hands get dirty, water washes them. When clothes are stained, soap cleans them. And when the mind is stained by wrongdoing, it is washed clean by love of the Name.
neighbors.difference: Rumi's Sufis polish the heart through remembrance of God and a teacher's guidance. For Sikhs, the cleansing comes through remembering the Name and the Guru's grace, lived in an ordinary household life.
neighbors.shared: every heart can be made clear again.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 4, Japji Sahib, pauri 20 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a soft answer
neighbors.text: Today Marcus said real kindness can't be beaten. The book of Proverbs says it in one line: "A soft answer turneth away wrath; But a grievous word stirreth up anger." And Proverbs goes further: if your enemy is hungry, give him bread to eat.
neighbors.difference: Marcus finds kindness invincible because it's what reason and human nature ask. In Proverbs, gentleness is wisdom from God, and the verse about feeding your enemy adds that the LORD will reward you.
neighbors.shared: a gentle answer can quiet a sharp moment.

neighbors.heading: an old rule
neighbors.text: Today Marcus met a sharp person gently, and refused to fight. The Dhammapada says it in Max Müller's words: "For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love—this is an old rule." Buddhists practice that love on purpose, until it holds even when someone is unkind.
neighbors.difference: Marcus gently corrects the person who wrongs him, as kin under one reason. For Buddhists, answering hate with love frees the heart from the anger that harms the one who holds it.
neighbors.shared: kindness can hold its ground without a fight.

neighbors.heading: little and often
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said to carry one thought from your reading all day. Muslims know that rhythm. The Qur'an calls itself a blessed scripture revealed "that they may ponder its revelations." And the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ taught that the deeds most loved by God are the ones kept up regularly, even if they're small.
neighbors.difference: Seneca reads a few good authors to grow wise. Muslims recite the Qur'an as the word of God, often in Arabic, as an act of worship as well as study.
neighbors.shared: a little every day goes further than a lot once.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 38:29 (Pickthall 1930) · Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, on small regular deeds (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: don't neglect study
neighbors.text: Today Seneca chose one thought a day to chew on. In the Taittiriya Upanishad, when a student finishes learning the Veda, the teacher sends him off with advice. Speak the truth. Follow dharma. And don't neglect study, svadhyaya: keep studying and reciting the sacred texts.
neighbors.difference: Seneca read to train his own reason. In the Upanishad, ongoing study keeps a person close to sacred teaching, a duty owed alongside honoring parents, teachers and guests.
neighbors.shared: learning doesn't end; it just becomes a daily habit.

neighbors.heading: the light in all
neighbors.text: Today namaste bowed to someone with both hands. Sikhs greet with joined hands too, saying Sat Sri Akal. And Guru Nanak sang a hymn many Sikhs still recite at night: in every one is the Light, and that Light is You. To see the Light in someone is to see the Creator there.
neighbors.difference: In Hindu thought, many hear namaste as bowing to the divine present in each person. Sikhs speak of one Creator's Light shining in all, while the Creator stays beyond what anyone can hold.
neighbors.shared: every person you greet carries something worth bowing to.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 13, Sohila, Guru Nanak (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: made in the image
neighbors.text: Today namaste bowed to the other person. Christians honor each person for a reason found on the Bible's first page: "So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them." Every face you meet bears that image.
neighbors.difference: Some Hindus hear namaste as honoring the sacred within each person. For Christians, people are not divine; they are made in God's image, which is why every one is precious.
neighbors.shared: every person you meet deserves your respect.

neighbors.heading: even under the saw
neighbors.text: Today you met metta, wishing all beings well. The Buddha tested it in one of his hardest images. Even if bandits sawed you limb from limb, he said, anyone who let hate fill their heart wouldn't be following his teaching. Keep a mind of goodwill, he urged, wide as the world, toward them too.
neighbors.difference: On this path, metta is borrowed as a practice you can try without the rest. For Buddhists, it belongs to the whole path to awakening, alongside ethics, wisdom and the community.
neighbors.shared: goodwill can reach even the one who's hard to love.
neighbors.sources: Majjhima Nikaya 21, the simile of the saw (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: love your enemies
neighbors.text: Today metta wished well even to someone difficult. Jesus asked the same of his followers: "But I say to you, Love your enemies: do good to them that hate you: and pray for them that persecute and calumniate you." Catholics are asked to pray for others, the hard ones included.
neighbors.difference: Metta is a heart trained to wish all beings well, with no creator behind it. Catholics love enemies because God loves them, and pray to God for them.
neighbors.shared: the hardest person to love is still worth wishing well.

neighbors.heading: the meal is an offering
neighbors.text: Today a blessing stopped to name the bread. Some Hindus pause before eating too, with a verse from the Bhagavad Gita: the offering is Brahman, the food is Brahman, offered by Brahman into the fire that is Brahman. A plate becomes an offering, and eating becomes a way of remembering.
neighbors.difference: Jewish blessings thank the one God, ruler of the universe, for each gift. The Gita verse sees the food, the eater and the act as all one sacred reality, Brahman.
neighbors.shared: a meal tastes different when you stop to notice it.

neighbors.heading: eat, be satisfied, bless
neighbors.text: Today you learned blessings before you eat. The Torah adds one after: "And thou shalt eat and be satisfied, and bless the LORD thy God for the good land which He hath given thee." From this verse comes the grace after meals, said when the plate is empty and the thanks is easiest to forget.
neighbors.difference: On this path, a blessing can be borrowed as a way of noticing. For Jews, it's a mitzvah, a commandment, words spoken to God and kept as part of a covenant.
neighbors.shared: thanks belongs at the end of the meal, too.

neighbors.heading: the whole law
neighbors.text: Today Jesus named two commandments that hold up all the rest. Paul put the second one plainly for the Christians in Rome: "Love worketh no ill to his neighbour: therefore love is the fulfilling of the law." Not a feeling to wait for, but a way to treat the person next to you.
neighbors.difference: On this path, love of neighbor can stand on its own. For Christians it can't be pulled apart from love of God, and both are rooted in God's love shown in Jesus.
neighbors.shared: love shows up in how we treat the person nearby.

neighbors.heading: what you love for yourself
neighbors.text: Today Jesus said to love your neighbor as yourself. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said something close: none of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself. And alongside it, the Qur'an keeps love and worship of the one God first.
neighbors.difference: Christians hear the two commandments in the words of Jesus, whom they call Lord. Muslims honor Jesus as a prophet, and follow the guidance given through the Prophet Muhammad.
neighbors.shared: wish for others the good you'd want for yourself.

neighbors.heading: go in peace?
neighbors.text: Today the works of mercy fed, clothed and visited. Saint James pictures someone without clothes or daily food, and a believer who says only: "Go in peace, be ye warmed and filled." What good is that, he asks, without the things the body needs? For Catholics, faith shows up in a meal and a coat.
neighbors.difference: On this path, mercy can be practiced for its own sake. Catholics see Christ himself in the person they serve, and serve as part of their faith in him.
neighbors.shared: kind words matter more when they come with a coat.

neighbors.heading: seva
neighbors.text: Today the works of mercy fed the hungry and visited the sick. Sikhs call that kind of help seva, selfless service: cooking in the langar, cleaning, caring for whoever comes. Guru Nanak sang that by serving in this world, a person finds a place of honor in the Lord's court.
neighbors.difference: Catholics serve Christ in the least of his brethren. Sikhs serve the one Creator whose Light is in everyone, and seva is done without seeking anything back.
neighbors.shared: serving someone in need is a holy thing.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 26, Guru Nanak (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: open thy hand
neighbors.text: Today zakat set aside a share for those in need. Jews have tzedakah, a word that also means justice: giving isn't only kindness, it's what's right. The Torah says: "Thou shalt surely open thy hand unto thy poor and needy brother, in thy land." Some Jewish homes keep a small box for coins.
neighbors.difference: Zakat has a set share and named recipients, one of Islam's five pillars. Jewish law has its own rules for tzedakah, and frames it as justice owed within the covenant.
neighbors.shared: what we give away was never only ours.

neighbors.heading: if they knew
neighbors.text: Today zakat taught that giving purifies the giver. Buddhists begin the path with dana, giving. The Buddha said that if people knew the fruit of sharing as he did, they wouldn't eat a meal without sharing it, even their last bite, if there were someone to receive it.
neighbors.difference: Zakat is a duty to Allah, with a set share. Dana is freely given, with no set amount, and it loosens the grip of craving on the way to freedom.
neighbors.shared: giving loosens the grip of not-enough.

neighbors.heading: for the love of him
neighbors.text: Today langar fed everyone, sitting side by side. The Qur'an praises those who "feed with food the needy wretch, the orphan and the prisoner, for love of Him," saying: "We wish for no reward nor thanks from you." At iftar in Ramadan, some mosques open their doors and share a meal with whoever comes.
neighbors.difference: Sikh langar is served every day, seated together on the floor to undo caste. In Islam, feeding others is worship of Allah, and community meals often gather around prayer and the fast.
neighbors.shared: a shared meal makes strangers a little less strange.

neighbors.heading: the guest is God
neighbors.text: Today langar fed whoever walked in. The Taittiriya Upanishad has an old line, atithi devo bhava: let the guest be as God to you. The same Upanishad teaches: don't turn away anyone who comes to your home, and gather food so you have something to give.
neighbors.difference: Langar is a community kitchen where caste is set aside. The Upanishad's teaching is about hospitality at home, honoring the guest as you would the divine.
neighbors.shared: whoever comes to your table is worth honoring.

neighbors.heading: a thief at the door
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said the jolt of anger isn't yet anger; agreeing with it is. Sikhs name krodh, anger, among five thieves that rob the mind, with lust, greed, attachment and ego. Guru Arjan's verse tells anger that compassion never rises in it. The answer is remembering the Name, and staying in rising spirits.
neighbors.difference: Seneca stops anger by reason, refusing to agree with the jolt. Sikhs guard against anger by remembering God's Name and keeping company with the Guru's word.
neighbors.shared: the flash isn't you; what you do next is.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, on the five thieves (paraphrase) · Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1358, Guru Arjan (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: be angry, and sin not
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said the jolt happens to you, but the yes is yours. Paul makes room for the same line: "Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath." The feeling may come, but don't let it settle in overnight. Some Christians end the day by letting go of a grudge.
neighbors.difference: Seneca wants a mind that doesn't agree to anger at all. Paul allows anger, asks that it not become sin, and lets God's forgiveness shape how Christians forgive.
neighbors.shared: a hard feeling can pass through you before sunset.

neighbors.heading: firm like a fortress
neighbors.text: Today Marcus called a calm mind a citadel. The Dhammapada uses a fortress too. Knowing the body is fragile like a clay jar, it says, make the mind firm "like a fortress," and meet Mara, the tempter, with wisdom. Buddhists guard the mind's gates with mindfulness, one moment at a time.
neighbors.difference: Marcus's citadel is reason free of runaway passion. For Buddhists, the guarded mind isn't a self to defend; it's a mind freeing itself from craving.
neighbors.shared: there's a steady place inside you worth returning to.

neighbors.heading: the interior castle
neighbors.text: Today Marcus called the quiet mind a citadel. The Spanish saint Teresa of Avila pictured the soul as a castle, made of a single diamond or clear crystal, with many rooms. Prayer is the door in, she wrote, and in the room at the very center, God lives.
neighbors.difference: Marcus walked back to a citadel of his own reason. For Teresa, the castle's center isn't the self but God, who waits there and draws the soul in.
neighbors.shared: there's a quiet room inside, and it's worth walking back to.
neighbors.sources: Teresa of Avila, The Interior Castle, first mansions, chapter 1 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: dawn and dusk
neighbors.text: Today the Stoic day began with a preview and ended with a review. Some Hindus frame the day too, with sandhya, prayers at the joining of night and day. At sunrise and at sunset, some recite the Gayatri mantra from the Rig Veda, asking the divine light to inspire their thinking.
neighbors.difference: The Stoics framed the day to train reason and character. Sandhya is worship, honoring the divine light at the turning points of the day.
neighbors.shared: the edges of the day are good places to pause.

neighbors.heading: morning and night
neighbors.text: Today the Stoic day had a morning, a middle and an evening. A psalm frames the day too: "To declare Thy lovingkindness in the morning, And Thy faithfulness in the night seasons." Jewish tradition has a waking prayer of thanks for a returned soul, and a bedtime Shema that can begin by forgiving anyone who hurt them.
neighbors.difference: Seneca reviewed his day before his own conscience. Jews bring the day to God, morning and night, in prayers the tradition sets.
neighbors.shared: begin with thanks, and end the day with forgiveness.
neighbors.sources: Psalm 92:3 (JPS 1917; 92:2 in many Bibles) · Modeh Ani and the bedtime Shema (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: arise and eat
neighbors.text: Today you heard that stopping is wisdom, not failure. The prophet Elijah once ran into the desert, worn out, and asked to die. An angel didn't scold him. It touched him and said: "Arise and eat; because the journey is too great for thee." Bread, water and sleep came first.
neighbors.difference: The study maps hard experiences and offers practical care. For Christians, God meets the exhausted with care too, and the story goes on to a still, small voice.
neighbors.shared: rest and help are part of the path, not a detour.

neighbors.heading: not beyond its scope
neighbors.text: Today you heard that hard passages happen, and stopping is okay. The Qur'an says: "Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope." Islam has its own ease built in: someone ill or traveling may make up missed fast days later, and someone who can't stand may pray sitting.
neighbors.difference: The researchers describe difficulties honestly and point to help. In Islam, ease comes from Allah's mercy, built into the law itself.
neighbors.shared: you're never asked to carry more than you can.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 2:286 (Pickthall 1930) · Qur'an 2:184–185 (paraphrase) · Sahih al-Bukhari 1117, on praying seated (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: two or three
neighbors.text: Today a study found that people are part of health. Jesus put company at the center of prayer: "For where there are two or three gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them." Catholics are called to gather at Sunday Mass, and some keep small groups that pray and share meals.
neighbors.difference: The study measures ties that help people live longer. For Catholics, gathering isn't only good for you; Christ promises to be present among them.
neighbors.shared: you're not meant to walk this path alone.

neighbors.heading: sangat
neighbors.text: Today the study said people are health. Sikhs call good company sangat, the gathering of seekers. Guru Nanak asked how to know true company, and answered: it's where the one Name is spoken. Sikhs sing together, eat together in the langar, and say a person is shaped by the company they keep.
neighbors.difference: The study counts social ties of every kind. For Sikhs, sangat is company gathered around God's Name and the Guru's word, not only friendship.
neighbors.shared: good company helps you become who you hope to be.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 72, Guru Nanak (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: out to the field
neighbors.text: Today a walk among trees quieted the mind. The Torah has a man walking out at dusk: "And Isaac went out to meditate in the field at the eventide." The rabbis read it as prayer. Centuries later, the Hasidic teacher Rebbe Nachman of Breslov urged people to speak with God alone in the fields.
neighbors.difference: The study looked for less brooding after a walk. For Isaac and Rebbe Nachman, the field is a place to speak with God, not only to rest the mind.
neighbors.shared: a quiet walk outside can make room inside.
neighbors.sources: Genesis 24:63 (JPS 1917) · Talmud, Berakhot 26b (paraphrase) · Rebbe Nachman, on hitbodedut (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: forests are delightful
neighbors.text: Today green places quieted a looping mind. The Buddha woke up under a tree, and often told his monks to meditate at the roots of trees. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's words: "Forests are delightful; where the world finds no delight, there the passionless will find delight."
neighbors.difference: The study measured a mood lift after a walk. For Buddhists, the forest is a place for practice, where a mind free of craving finds a quiet joy.
neighbors.shared: the trees are patient company for a busy mind.

neighbors.heading: increase me in knowledge
neighbors.text: Today Socrates and Nicholas of Cusa honored knowing what you don't know. The Qur'an says: "and of knowledge ye have been vouchsafed but little." And it gives a short prayer for the gap: "My Lord! Increase me in knowledge." Muslim scholars often closed an answer with Allahu a'lam, God knows best.
neighbors.difference: This path leaves the answers open for you to choose. In Islam, the answers belong to Allah and were revealed, and the humility is before him.
neighbors.shared: it's okay to say I don't know, and keep learning.

neighbors.heading: perhaps he knows
neighbors.text: Today you made a list of what you still don't know. A hymn in the Rig Veda does the same. The Rig Veda's hymn of creation asks where everything came from, and ends on a question: the one who watches over it in the highest heaven surely knows, or perhaps even he does not know.
neighbors.difference: This path asks you to live the questions. The hymn is part of the Vedas, sacred scripture, and Hindu traditions answer it in many ways, often with the one reality, Brahman.
neighbors.shared: an honest question can be as sacred as an answer.

neighbors.heading: look back, rise up
neighbors.text: Today you looked back down the hill, then up. Sikhs do something like it in Ardas, the prayer that closes many gatherings. It remembers the Gurus and those who gave their lives, one by one, then asks for the Name, and ends with chardi kala, rising spirits, and the good of all.
neighbors.difference: This path looks back on your own year. Ardas looks back on the Guru's whole community, and lifts it up to Waheguru, the Wondrous Lord.
neighbors.shared: remembering where you've been helps you rise to what's next.

neighbors.heading: hitherto
neighbors.text: Today you stood at a lookout and saw how far you'd come. The prophet Samuel once set up a stone to remember a hard road: "Then Samuel took a stone… and called the name of it Ebenezer, saying, Hitherto hath the LORD helped us." Some Christians still sing of raising their Ebenezer.
neighbors.difference: This path celebrates your own steps. Samuel's stone says it was God who helped them this far, and Christians look back to give thanks to him.
neighbors.shared: it's good to mark how far you've come.

neighbors.heading: a mustard seed
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said: never say "I lost it," say "I gave it back." Buddhists tell of Kisa Gotami, who carried her dead little son from house to house, looking for medicine. The Buddha asked her for one mustard seed from a home where no one had ever died. She found none, and came to see that everything that comes into being also passes.
neighbors.difference: Epictetus pictures a giver who lends and takes back. The Buddha names no lender: all that arises passes away, and the way through grief is to stop clinging, even to a self that owns things.
neighbors.shared: you can hold what you love with open hands.
neighbors.sources: Dhammapada Commentary, the story of Kisa Gotami (verse 114) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the lord gave
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said: never say "I lost it," say "I gave it back." Catholics know an older voice. When Job lost his children and everything he had, he said: "The Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away: as it hath pleased the Lord so is it done: blessed be the name of the Lord."
neighbors.difference: Epictetus asks for calm. Job first tore his garment and fell to the ground, and later cried out and argued with God. Catholics read Job as a man of faith who could grieve aloud before God.
neighbors.shared: the people we love are a gift, not a possession.

neighbors.heading: enjoy by letting go
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said to live as at a banquet: take a modest share, and don't reach after the dish that passes. The Isha Upanishad opens in a similar key. All of this, it says, is covered by the Lord; enjoy it by letting go, and don't covet anyone's wealth.
neighbors.difference: Epictetus keeps desire small because the dish isn't up to you. The Upanishad sees the whole world filled with the Lord, so what you enjoy is received, not grabbed.
neighbors.shared: a modest share, received gladly, is a full meal.

neighbors.heading: rejoicing in your portion
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said to live as at a banquet: take a modest share, and don't reach after the dish that passes. The rabbis asked about the same table. Ben Zoma said: who is rich? The one who rejoices in his portion. And the Torah says: "thou shalt eat and be satisfied, and bless the LORD thy God."
neighbors.difference: Epictetus asks for restraint, so desire can't rule you. Jewish tradition adds thanks: a blessing before eating and after, because the food comes from God, and a portion received with joy honors him.
neighbors.shared: a modest plate, met with joy, is a full one.

neighbors.heading: the other cheek
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said an insult only harms you if you judge that it has. Jesus taught: "whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also." And he went further: "Love your enemies, bless them that curse you."
neighbors.difference: Epictetus guards your judgment, so the blow can't reach the inside. Jesus doesn't say the blow is nothing; he asks you to answer it with love, even to pray for the one who struck, as children of a Father kind to all.
neighbors.shared: an insult doesn't get to decide who you become.

neighbors.heading: answer: peace
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said an insult only harms you if you judge that it has. The Qur'an describes the servants of the Merciful: they walk the earth modestly, "and when the foolish ones address them answer: Peace." It also says: "Repel the evil deed with one which is better," and an enemy may become a warm friend.
neighbors.difference: Epictetus treats the insult as finished inside your own judgment. The Qur'an allows a fair answer to a wrong, yet calls pardoning and making peace better, and says its reward is with God.
neighbors.shared: you can answer a sharp word with peace.

neighbors.heading: reckon the charges
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said to look at what comes before and after anything you start, like an athlete before the games. Jesus told the crowds following him: "which of you having a mind to build a tower, doth not first sit down, and reckon the charges that are necessary, whether he have wherewithal to finish it."
neighbors.difference: Epictetus asks whether your own strength is enough. In Luke, the cost is following Jesus with your whole life, and Catholics trust that God's grace helps them pay what they couldn't alone.
neighbors.shared: a promise kept starts with an honest look at its cost.

neighbors.heading: head on your palm
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said to count the cost before you begin, like an athlete before the games. Guru Nanak set the price of his path just as plainly: if you want to play the game of love, come to my lane with your head on your palm.
neighbors.difference: Epictetus counts the cost so you won't quit in shame halfway. For Guru Nanak, the price is the ego itself, laid down in love for God, and it's God's grace that makes it possible.
neighbors.shared: the deepest things ask for your whole heart.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1412, Guru Nanak (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: not a talebearer
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said to speak rarely, only what's needed, and not about people. The Torah says: "Thou shalt not go up and down as a talebearer among thy people." And in the Mishnah, Shimon, son of Rabban Gamliel, says he grew up among the sages and found nothing better for the body than silence.
neighbors.difference: Epictetus keeps quiet to guard his own character. Jewish law also counts the harm to the one spoken about, and treats hurtful talk, even when true, as a wrong against a neighbor and before God.
neighbors.shared: a quiet tongue is a kindness to people not in the room.

neighbors.heading: the right time, the true word
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said to speak rarely, only what's needed, and not about people. The Buddha taught right speech. A word is well spoken, he said, when it's spoken at the right time, it's true, it's gentle, it's helpful, and it comes from a mind of goodwill.
neighbors.difference: Epictetus makes silence the general rule. The Buddha's test isn't how little you say but what kind of word it is, and right speech is one step on the path to freedom from suffering.
neighbors.shared: before you speak, ask if it's true and if it's kind.

neighbors.heading: eat, and be not prodigal
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said the body is the measure of what you need, as the foot is of the shoe. The Qur'an says: "eat and drink, but be not prodigal. Lo! He loveth not the prodigals." And a hadith gives a picture: a third of the stomach for food, a third for drink, a third for breath.
neighbors.difference: Epictetus lets the body set the limit. The Qur'an treats food as God's good provision, to enjoy with thanks; keeping to measure honors the Giver.
neighbors.shared: enough is a gift you can say thank you for.

neighbors.heading: not too much, not too little
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said the body is the measure of what you need, as the foot is of the shoe. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says yoga isn't for someone who eats too much or too little, or sleeps too much or too little. For one who is measured in food, rest and work, he says, yoga ends sorrow.
neighbors.difference: Epictetus measures need so the will stays free. Krishna's measure serves yoga: a steady body and mind, so a person can turn inward and toward God.
neighbors.shared: the body knows when it's enough; listen kindly.

neighbors.heading: truthful living
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said sheep don't show the shepherd how much they ate; they show wool. Don't talk about your principles; live them. Guru Nanak said it in one line: truth is higher than everything, but higher still is truthful living.
neighbors.difference: Epictetus wants deeds over talk so you won't be a showman. For Guru Nanak, truthful living grows from remembering God's Name, and it's lived in an ordinary life of honest work and sharing.
neighbors.shared: people learn more from how you live than from what you say.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 62, Guru Nanak (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: by their fruits
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said sheep don't show the shepherd how much they ate; they show wool. Don't talk about your principles; live them. Jesus used a tree for the same idea: "Ye shall know them by their fruits." And the letter of James says: "shew me thy faith without thy works, and I will shew thee my faith by my works."
neighbors.difference: For Epictetus, deeds show a mind trained by reason. For Christians, good fruit grows from faith in Christ and the Spirit at work; works show faith, they don't earn God's love.
neighbors.shared: let your life say what words can't.

neighbors.heading: the simile of the saw
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said a tyrant can chain his leg, but not even Zeus can conquer his will. The Buddha gave a harder picture. Even if bandits were cutting you limb from limb with a saw, he said, anyone whose mind turned to hatred wouldn't be following his teaching. Keep the mind unshaken, and full of goodwill, even toward them.
neighbors.difference: Epictetus holds the will as his own, out of anyone's reach. The Buddha asks for more than firmness: goodwill toward the one doing harm, and he doesn't treat the mind as a self you own.
neighbors.shared: what's deepest in you can't be chained.

neighbors.heading: they cannot kill the soul
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said a tyrant can chain his leg, but not even Zeus can conquer his will. Jesus told his friends: "fear ye not them that kill the body, and are not able to kill the soul." The Church remembers martyrs who stood calm before rulers, trusting that what mattered most was safe.
neighbors.difference: For Epictetus, the will is free by its own nature. Catholics say the soul is safe because God holds it, the God who notices every sparrow; that freedom is a gift kept in his hands.
neighbors.shared: the deepest part of you can't be locked away.

neighbors.heading: the same in all
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus told a master: your slave is your brother, born of the same Zeus. The Bhagavad Gita says the wise see the same in a learned Brahmin, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and an outcaste. Krishna says the yogi sees the Self in every being, and every being in the Self.
neighbors.difference: Epictetus finds kinship in the reason every person shares. The Gita sees one Self in all beings, animals too, and teaches that seeing it changes how you treat everyone.
neighbors.shared: no one is beneath you; everyone is kin.

neighbors.heading: one father
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus told a master: your slave is your brother, born of the same Zeus. A Hebrew prophet asked the same question: "Have we not all one father? Hath not one God created us? Why do we deal treacherously every man against his brother?"
neighbors.difference: Epictetus's Zeus is the reason running through nature. Malachi's one father is the one God who created each person, and the Torah gave servants the Sabbath's rest too.
neighbors.shared: the one who serves you is your brother or sister.

neighbors.heading: the temple within
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said that when you shut the door and darken the room, you're not alone: God is within. Paul wrote to the Christians at Corinth: "Know ye not that ye are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you?" And Jesus promised: "lo, I am with you alway."
neighbors.difference: For Epictetus, God is the reason running through all things, present in each of us. Christians speak of the Holy Spirit dwelling in believers: a personal God who knows and loves them by name.
neighbors.shared: even in a dark, quiet room, you're not alone.

neighbors.heading: nearer than the jugular
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said that when you shut the door and darken the room, you're not alone. The Qur'an says of every person: "We know what his soul whispereth to him, and We are nearer to him than his jugular vein." And: "He is with you wheresoever ye may be."
neighbors.difference: Epictetus says God is within you, a share of the divine. In Islam, God is closer than your own vein in knowing and care, yet never part of you; the Creator stays One, beyond all he made.
neighbors.shared: no door shuts you away from being known.

neighbors.heading: virtue is a habit
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said every habit grows by the actions that match it: walk to become a walker. The Catholic Church teaches the same about goodness. Its Catechism calls virtue a habitual and firm disposition to do good, and says human virtues are gained by education, deliberate acts and perseverance, again and again.
neighbors.difference: Epictetus builds character by practice alone. Catholics say that too for human virtues, but faith, hope and love are gifts poured in by God's grace, which also helps the practice along.
neighbors.shared: every small good act makes the next one easier.

neighbors.heading: you sow, you eat
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said every habit grows by the actions that match it: walk to become a walker. In the Japji, Guru Nanak says good and bad aren't just words we say; our deeds are written down, and what we sow, we ourselves eat. When the mind is soiled, he says, love of God's Name washes it clean.
neighbors.difference: Epictetus says practice alone makes you who you are. Guru Nanak gives deeds real weight, but says the door of liberation opens by God's grace, not by effort alone.
neighbors.shared: what you practice today, you become.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 2 and Ang 4, Japji 4 and 20, Guru Nanak (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: love that doesn't depend
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said friendship fails when two people want the same piece of meat. The Mishnah says something close: love that depends on a thing ends when the thing is gone; love that depends on nothing never ends. Its example of the lasting kind is David and Jonathan, whose souls, the Bible says, were knit together.
neighbors.difference: Epictetus says only those who place the good in their own will can be friends. David and Jonathan sealed their friendship as a covenant before God, a bond held by faithfulness, not only by right judgment.
neighbors.shared: a real friend wants you, not what you can give.

neighbors.heading: the good friend
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said friendship fails when two people want the same piece of meat. The Buddha told a young man named Sigala how to tell friends apart. The false friend only takes, or only flatters. The true one helps, stays the same in good times and bad, tells you what's good for you, and cares.
neighbors.difference: Epictetus sees friendship as the fruit of a mind already set right. The Buddha called good friendship the whole of the holy life: not only the reward of the path, but part of how you walk it.
neighbors.shared: a real friend wants you, not what you can give.
neighbors.sources: Digha Nikaya 31, Sigalovada Sutta; Samyutta Nikaya 45.2 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: every post a trust
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said each life is like military service: one stands guard, one scouts, and you stay at the post you've been given. The Qur'an says God has placed people as viceroys of the earth, "and hath exalted some of you in rank above others, that He may try you by (the test of) that which He hath given you."
neighbors.difference: Epictetus asks you to trust the general and serve well. In the Qur'an, every post is a trust and a test from God, and each person answers to him for how they used what they were given.
neighbors.shared: there's no small post when it's held faithfully.

neighbors.heading: your own duty
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said to stay at the post you've been given, like a soldier. The Bhagavad Gita begins with a real soldier, Arjuna, wanting to leave his post. Krishna tells him: better your own duty, even done imperfectly, than another's done well.
neighbors.difference: Epictetus serves at his post because the general knows best. Krishna asks Arjuna to act without clinging to the results, offering the work itself to God, so the post becomes a path to freedom.
neighbors.shared: there's no small post when it's held faithfully.

neighbors.heading: contentment holds the earth
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said the poor person isn't the one with too little, but the one who craves more. Guru Nanak's Japji has an old picture: the bull said to hold up the earth is dharma, born of compassion, and contentment holds it patiently in place.
neighbors.difference: Seneca reasons his way to wanting less. For Sikhs, contentment grows from living in God's will and remembering the Name, by grace, and it goes hand in hand with honest work and sharing.
neighbors.shared: enough, held gladly, makes anyone rich.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 3, Japji 16, Guru Nanak (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: learned to be content
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said the poor person isn't the one with too little, but the one who craves more. Paul wrote, while in chains: "I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content." And to Timothy: "godliness with contentment is great gain."
neighbors.difference: Seneca finds contentment in a mind that needs nothing more. Paul names where his strength comes from: "I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me."
neighbors.shared: enough, held gladly, makes anyone rich.

neighbors.heading: from craving, fear
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said hope and fear are chained together, like a prisoner and his guard. The Dhammapada traces both to one root: "From greed comes grief, from greed comes fear; he who is free from greed knows neither grief nor fear."
neighbors.difference: Seneca's cure is to live in the present and stop leaning on tomorrow. The Buddha's is the ending of craving itself, which the path loosens step by step, until even clinging to a self that hopes falls away.
neighbors.shared: this moment is a safe place to stand.

neighbors.heading: sufficient for the day
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said hope and fear are chained together: both run ahead to tomorrow. Jesus told the crowds: "Be not therefore solicitous for to morrow; for the morrow will be solicitous for itself. Sufficient for the day is the evil thereof."
neighbors.difference: Seneca says stop hoping and you'll stop fearing. Catholics keep hope as a virtue, one of three God gives, but move it off tomorrow's outcomes and onto God himself.
neighbors.shared: today has enough in it; let tomorrow wait.
neighbors.sources: Matthew 6:34 (Douay-Rheims); Catechism of the Catholic Church 1817 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the witness within
neighbors.text: Today Seneca passed on a rule: live among people as if God saw you. The Shvetashvatara Upanishad speaks of one God hidden in all beings, filling everything, the inner Self of all, who watches over every deed: the witness.
neighbors.difference: Seneca's rule is a practice, living as if watched. For the Upanishad, the witness isn't an eye outside you; it's the one God, the inner Self of every being.
neighbors.shared: live the same whether or not anyone's looking.

neighbors.heading: an eye that sees
neighbors.text: Today Seneca passed on a rule: live among people as if God saw you. The Mishnah says it without the "as if": know what is above you, an eye that sees, an ear that hears, and all your deeds written in a book. Keep that in mind, it says, and you won't fall into wrongdoing.
neighbors.difference: For Seneca, the watcher is a picture that helps. For the Mishnah, God truly sees and remembers, and Jewish tradition holds that the same God welcomes return and forgives.
neighbors.shared: be the same person in the dark as in the light.

neighbors.heading: i die daily
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said we die every day: each day, a little of life is taken away. Paul wrote almost the same words to the Christians at Corinth: "I die daily." He meant he faced danger every day for the gospel, and he wrote it in a chapter about rising again.
neighbors.difference: Seneca counts the days so we'll use them well and fear the end less. Paul faces each day's dying in the hope of resurrection: "O death, where is thy sting?"
neighbors.shared: each day is a gift; spend it on what matters.

neighbors.heading: a stranger, a traveler
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said we die every day, so treat each one as precious. The Prophet Muhammad told Ibn Umar: be in this world as if you were a stranger, or a traveler passing through. Ibn Umar added: in the evening, don't wait for the morning; take from your health for your sickness, and from your life for your death.
neighbors.difference: Seneca leaves open what comes after. For Muslims, the traveler is going home to God, and the days given here are a trust to fill with good, to be met again in the Hereafter.
neighbors.shared: travel light, and use today well.

neighbors.heading: more inward than my inmost
