neighbors.text: Today Seneca wrote: "God is near you, he is with you, he is within you." Saint Augustine, writing his Confessions as a prayer, found the same nearness. He said to God: "Thou wert more inward to me than my most inward part; and higher than my highest."
neighbors.difference: Seneca's god within sounds like a share of divine reason in us. For Augustine, God is closer than our inmost self yet higher than our highest: the Creator, never a part of us.
neighbors.shared: you're closer to the holy than you know.

neighbors.heading: you are light
neighbors.text: Today Seneca wrote that God is near you, with you, within you. Guru Amar Das speaks to his own mind: O my mind, you are the very form of divine light; know your source. And Guru Nanak sings that one light is in everyone, and that light is God's.
neighbors.difference: Seneca reaches the god within by reason and a good character. In Sikh teaching, the light is in all, and it's recognized through the Guru's word and remembering God's Name, by grace.
neighbors.shared: there's a light in you, and in everyone you meet.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 441, Guru Amar Das; Ang 13, Guru Nanak (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: remember egypt
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said: treat those beneath you as you'd want to be treated by those above. The Torah grounds the same care in memory: "And thou shalt remember that thou wast a bondman in the land of Egypt." And Hillel taught: what is hateful to you, don't do to your neighbor; that is the whole Torah.
neighbors.difference: Seneca reminds you that fortune could flip. The Torah gives a story and a command: you were slaves, God freed you, so treat the stranger and the servant as one who remembers.
neighbors.shared: remember when you were small, and be kind to the small.

neighbors.heading: they are like you
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said: treat those beneath you as you'd want to be treated by those above. The Dhammapada puts it in the plainest terms: "All men tremble at punishment, all men fear death; remember that you are like unto them, and do not kill, nor cause slaughter."
neighbors.difference: Seneca argues from fortune, which could put you below tomorrow. The Buddha argues from the fear of pain we all share, and widens the circle past people, to every living being.
neighbors.shared: everyone fears pain just as you do; be gentle.

neighbors.heading: the bee's path
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said to read like the bees: gather from many flowers, then make honey that is your own. The Qur'an has a chapter named The Bee. God inspires the bee to "eat of all fruits, and follow the ways of thy Lord," and from it comes "a drink divers of hues, wherein is healing for mankind."
neighbors.difference: Seneca's bee is a picture of reading and blending. In the Qur'an the bee is a sign: it follows paths its Lord made smooth, and the honey calls people to reflect on him.
neighbors.shared: gather the good wherever it grows.

neighbors.heading: the bee and the scriptures
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said to read like the bees: gather from many flowers, then make honey that is your own. The Bhagavata Purana tells of a wandering sage who learned from the world around him, the bee among his teachers. As the bee takes nectar from many flowers, he says, the wise take the essence from every teaching, great and small.
neighbors.difference: Seneca's honey is your own good judgment. For the Bhagavata, the essence gathered is knowledge of the Self and love of God, and the sage's freedom comes from that, not from reading alone.
neighbors.shared: gather the good wherever it grows.

neighbors.heading: children of the one
neighbors.text: Today Seneca wrote: we are the limbs of one great body; nature made us kin. Guru Arjan sang: the One is our father, and we are all the One's children. Sikhs live it at the langar, the free kitchen, where everyone sits together on the floor and eats the same meal.
neighbors.difference: Seneca's kinship comes from nature, which made us of the same stuff. For Sikhs, it comes from one Creator, and it's lived out in seva, service, to anyone who walks in.
neighbors.shared: everyone at the table is family.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 611, Guru Arjan (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: many members, one body
neighbors.text: Today Seneca wrote: we are the limbs of one great body. Paul used the same picture for the church: "For as the body is one, and hath many members... so also is Christ." And: "whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it; or one member be honoured, all the members rejoice with it."
neighbors.difference: Seneca's body is all of humankind, joined by nature. Paul's body is Christ's, joined by the Spirit, though Christians also hold that every person is made in God's image.
neighbors.shared: when one of us hurts, we all do.

neighbors.heading: the best riches
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said the rich person is the one who has little and wants nothing more. The Dhammapada says: "Health is the greatest of gifts, contentedness the best riches; trust is the best of relationships, Nirvana the highest happiness."
neighbors.difference: Seneca's riches are a mind that needs nothing more. The Dhammapada sets contentment beside a further goal, Nirvana, the end of craving and suffering, which the path walks toward.
neighbors.shared: the best things you own can't be carried in a parade.

neighbors.heading: treasure in heaven
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said the rich person is the one who has little and wants nothing more. Jesus said: "Lay not up to yourselves treasures on earth: where the rust, and moth consume, and where thieves break through and steal." Store treasure in heaven instead, he said, "For where thy treasure is, there is thy heart also."
neighbors.difference: Seneca keeps his riches inside, in a mind content with little. Jesus points the heart toward God, and Catholics see giving to the poor as one way of storing up that treasure.
neighbors.shared: what your heart treasures is what you truly have.

neighbors.heading: bring the mind back
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said restless people keep changing places, fleeing themselves. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna gives Arjuna a gentle practice: wherever the restless, unsteady mind wanders off, draw it back, and let it rest in the Self.
neighbors.difference: Seneca's cure is to make peace with your own company. Krishna's is to come home to the Self, which the Gita teaches is deeper than the restless mind, and to God.
neighbors.shared: you can stop running and come home to yourself.

neighbors.heading: whither shall i flee
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said restless people keep changing places, fleeing themselves. Jonah tried running too; he "rose up to flee unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD." And a psalm asks: "Whither shall I go from Thy spirit? Or whither shall I flee from Thy presence?"
neighbors.difference: Seneca says you can't outrun yourself. The psalmist finds you can't outrun God, and takes comfort in it: even at the far end of the sea, "even there would Thy hand lead me."
neighbors.shared: you can stop running; what you need is already here.

neighbors.heading: slow to wrath
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said the greatest remedy for anger is delay. The letter of James says: "let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath: For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God." And Paul: "let not the sun go down upon your wrath."
neighbors.difference: Seneca wants anger gone entirely. Paul writes "Be ye angry, and sin not," so anger isn't always wrong; the danger is holding on to it, and his cure is forgiving as God forgave you.
neighbors.shared: a pause between the spark and the words is a gift.

neighbors.heading: sit down, then lie down
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said the greatest remedy for anger is delay. The Qur'an praises "those who control their wrath and are forgiving toward mankind." And the Prophet Muhammad gave a practical tip: if you're angry while standing, sit down; if the anger hasn't left, lie down.
neighbors.difference: Seneca's delay lets reason judge calmly. The Qur'an pairs holding back anger with forgiving, and says God loves those who do good.
neighbors.shared: a pause between the spark and the words is a gift.

neighbors.heading: the mote and the beam
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said that if we look honestly at our own faults, we'll be gentler with others'. Jesus asked: "why seest thou the mote that is in thy brother's eye; and seest not the beam that is in thy own eye?" And: "Judge not, and you shall not be judged."
neighbors.difference: Seneca's reason is fairness: no one could be acquitted of everything. Jesus adds mercy: forgive, and you will be forgiven, because God's mercy toward us is the measure for ours.
neighbors.shared: go easy on others; you've needed grace too.

neighbors.heading: i am the worst of all
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said that if we look honestly at our own faults, we'll be gentler with others'. Kabir, whose verses are in the Sikh scripture, says: of all people, I am the bad one; everyone but me is good. Whoever understands it this way, he says, is my friend.
neighbors.difference: Seneca's honesty about faults is a matter of fair judgment. In Sikh teaching, humility like Kabir's is part of devotion: the ego steps aside so God's love can fill the heart.
neighbors.shared: go easy on others; you've needed grace too.

neighbors.heading: giving as justice
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said to give freely, promptly, and without reminding. Maimonides set out the ways of giving tzedakah, from lower to higher. Higher is giving gladly, giving before you're asked, giving so neither side knows the other; highest is helping someone stand on their own, with a gift, a loan, or work.
neighbors.difference: For Seneca, a benefit is a free favor that binds friends. Tzedakah shares its root with the Hebrew word for justice: giving to the poor is a duty owed, not only a kindness.
neighbors.shared: give with an open hand and a quiet mouth.
neighbors.sources: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Gifts to the Poor 10:7-14 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the good person's gift
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said to give freely, promptly, and without reminding. The Buddha described a good person's gift: given with trust, given with care, given at the right time, given with a heart that doesn't cling, and given without hurting yourself or anyone else.
neighbors.difference: Seneca's benefit ties giver and receiver together in gratitude. In the Buddha's teaching, giving, dana, is practice in letting go, loosening craving in the one who gives.
neighbors.shared: give with an open hand and a quiet mouth.

neighbors.heading: steady when it's hard
neighbors.text: Today Marcus thanked a teacher for showing him how to stay the same person through sharp pain, long illness, even losing a child. Muslims call that steadiness sabr, patience. The Qur'an says believers will be tried with fear, hunger and loss, and gives glad tidings to the steadfast, "Who say, when a misfortune striketh them: Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning."
neighbors.difference: For Marcus, steadiness comes from judging rightly what can and can't harm the mind. For Muslims, patience is trust in God, who tests and sees, and the one who is lost is returning to Him too.
neighbors.shared: you can grieve and still be yourself.

neighbors.heading: the same in heat and cold
neighbors.text: Today Marcus learned to be the same through pain, grief and long illness. Hindus hear Krishna in that. In the Gita he tells Arjuna that the touch of the senses brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain; they come and go, so bear them. The one who stays the same in pleasure and pain, he says, is fit for the deathless.
neighbors.difference: Marcus steadies himself as a reasoning part of nature. Krishna grounds it in the self that is never born and never dies, beneath the body that feels the pain.
neighbors.shared: pain comes and goes; you can stay.

neighbors.heading: no harsh word
neighbors.text: Today Marcus remembered a teacher who never pounced on a mistake, just said the right word gently in the next sentence. Sikhs keep a line from Baba Farid in their scripture: don't speak even one harsh word, for the True Lord lives in everyone. Don't break anyone's heart; each one is a priceless jewel.
neighbors.difference: His teacher's gentleness was good teaching and good manners. For Sikhs, a harsh word wounds a heart where God dwells, so kindness in speech is also reverence.
neighbors.shared: nobody needs to be made small to learn.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Salok Farid (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: between you and him alone
neighbors.text: Today Marcus remembered a teacher who corrected people without making them small in front of others. Jesus gave his followers a similar way: "go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone: if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother." The point isn't winning the argument. It's keeping the person.
neighbors.difference: Marcus's teacher corrected a slip of grammar. Jesus is speaking of a brother who has done wrong, and the aim is to restore him, within the community of faith.
neighbors.shared: correct quietly, and you keep the friend.

neighbors.heading: your own field
neighbors.text: Today Marcus said few are unhappy for missing what's in someone else's mind, but whoever ignores their own is bound to be. The Dhammapada points the flashlight the same way: "Not the perversities of others, not their sins of commission or omission, but his own misdeeds and negligences should a sage take notice of."
neighbors.difference: Marcus watches the mind so its judgments stay true to reason and nature. In the Buddha's teaching, watching the mind is part of a path toward freedom from craving.
neighbors.shared: the one mind you can tend is yours.

neighbors.heading: the inner room
neighbors.text: Today Marcus told himself to follow the movements of his own mind. Catholics call that interiority. The Catechism says each person needs to be present enough to themselves to hear their conscience, and notes how life distracts us from reflection and self-examination. Catholics are encouraged to examine their conscience, often at the day's end.
neighbors.difference: For Marcus, the mind's ruling part is reason. For Catholics, conscience is where a person is alone with God, whose voice echoes there, and the examen ends in sorrow, thanks and trust in mercy.
neighbors.shared: a little quiet inside makes you safer to be around.

neighbors.heading: life may go, not the word
neighbors.text: Today Marcus said nothing is worth having if it makes you break your word. Hindus tell it in the Ramayana: Rama leaves for fourteen years of forest exile so his father's promise won't be broken. Tulsidas sings the family's way: in Raghu's line, life may go, but the word must not.
neighbors.difference: Marcus keeps his word to keep a self he can respect. In the Ramayana, keeping the word is dharma, and Rama, for many Hindus, is God living it out in a human life.
neighbors.shared: a word that holds in small things holds in big ones.
neighbors.sources: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda; Tulsidas, Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kanda (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: all that comes out of his mouth
neighbors.text: Today Marcus said never value what would force you to break your word. The Torah puts it plainly about vows: a person "shall not break his word; he shall do according to all that proceedeth out of his mouth." Jewish tradition takes words so seriously that the eve of Yom Kippur opens with Kol Nidre, about vows.
neighbors.difference: Marcus's test is self-respect and the bond between people. In the Torah, a vow is made to God, so keeping it is between the person and God too.
neighbors.shared: what you say is something you keep.

neighbors.heading: one blood
neighbors.text: Today Marcus reasoned that if we all share reason, we're fellow citizens of one city: the world. Paul said something close to the philosophers of Athens, Stoics among them. God, he said, "hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth."
neighbors.difference: Marcus's one city rests on reason shared by every mind. Paul's rests on one Creator, and he goes on to call his hearers to turn to God through Jesus.
neighbors.shared: the stranger at the bus stop is family.

neighbors.heading: that ye may know one another
neighbors.text: Today Marcus called the whole world one city, every stranger a fellow citizen. The Qur'an speaks to all people at once: "O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another." Then it says the noblest is the one best in conduct.
neighbors.difference: Marcus finds our kinship in shared reason. The Qur'an finds it in being created by one God, and the honor that counts is weighed by God, not by city or tribe.
neighbors.shared: born in different places, made to know one another.

neighbors.heading: remember your last end
neighbors.text: Today Marcus told himself not to act as if he'd live ten thousand years: while you can, be good. Catholics have an old book of wisdom with the same nudge: "In all thy works remember thy last end, and thou shalt never sin." Memento mori, remember you will die, is an old Catholic practice.
neighbors.difference: For Marcus, remembering death sorts what matters now. For Catholics, the last end also means judgment and the hope of heaven, so remembering it is a turn toward God's mercy.
neighbors.shared: later isn't promised, so do the good today.

neighbors.heading: this is your chance
neighbors.text: Today Marcus said death hangs over you, so be good while it's in your power. Sikhs hear Guru Arjan's line in their evening prayer: you've been given this human body; this is your chance to meet the Lord of the universe. Other work won't help, he says. Join the holy company and remember the Name.
neighbors.difference: Marcus's urgency is to act well before life ends. Guru Arjan's is to use this human birth to meet God and be free of coming and going.
neighbors.shared: this life is the chance; don't save the good for later.

neighbors.heading: seven times
neighbors.text: Today Marcus said the practice isn't never falling, it's coming back. Proverbs says it in one line: "For a righteous man falleth seven times, and riseth up again." Jewish tradition has a word for the coming back: teshuvah, return. It's open every day, not just once a year.
neighbors.difference: Marcus returns to philosophy the way sore eyes return to a soothing compress. Teshuvah is a return to God and the commandments, and to the people you've wronged.
neighbors.shared: falling isn't the end of the story; getting up is.

neighbors.heading: the moon from clouds
neighbors.text: Today Marcus told himself not to be disgusted when he slips, just come back. The Dhammapada has a picture for it: "He who formerly was reckless and afterwards became sober, brightens up this world, like the moon when freed from clouds." People who sit to meditate often learn it too: the mind wanders, you come back to the breath.
neighbors.difference: Marcus returns to living by reason and nature. In the Buddha's teaching, returning is training the mind on a path out of suffering, with no God being returned to.
neighbors.shared: you come back. that's the whole practice.

neighbors.heading: repel it with better
neighbors.text: Today Marcus said the best revenge is not to become like the wrongdoer. The Qur'an goes a step further: "Repel the evil deed with one which is better, then lo! he, between whom and thee there was enmity (will become) as though he was a bosom friend." The answer to harm isn't a mirror. It's something better.
neighbors.difference: Marcus guards his own character. The Qur'an also allows a just answer to a wrong, while holding up patience and the better deed, and hopes the enemy becomes a friend.
neighbors.shared: you don't have to become what hurt you.

neighbors.heading: free from anger
neighbors.text: Today Marcus kept the word revenge and changed what winning means: you stay the size you were. In the Gita, Krishna lists the qualities of one born to the divine nature. Among them: not harming, truthfulness, freedom from anger, gentleness, forgiveness, no malice. It's a picture of someone a wrong can't remake.
neighbors.difference: Marcus guards the one thing he thinks is truly his, his character. Krishna names these qualities as the divine nature, which leads toward liberation.
neighbors.shared: their rudeness doesn't get to rearrange you.

neighbors.heading: the lotus in the water
neighbors.text: Today Marcus did his duty at court but kept going home to philosophy. Sikhs live a householder's life too: working, raising families, serving. Guru Nanak's picture: as the lotus floats untouched on the water and the duck swims through the stream, so one whose mind rests on the Word crosses the world's ocean.
neighbors.difference: Marcus rests in philosophy to bear the court. For Sikhs, the anchor is the Word and the Name of God, remembered in the middle of ordinary work.
neighbors.shared: you can serve the world and still have a home inside.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 938, Sidh Gosht (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: in the world, not of it
neighbors.text: Today Marcus served the court faithfully and kept returning to what fed him. Jesus prayed something like that for his friends: "I pray not that thou shouldest take them out of the world, but that thou shouldest keep them from the evil. They are not of the world, even as I am not of the world."
neighbors.difference: Marcus's home is philosophy, a practice he returns to. In this prayer, the keeping comes from God, and Christians belong to Christ while they stay in the world.
neighbors.shared: stay in the work; keep going home.

neighbors.heading: when this is, that is
neighbors.text: Today Marcus said all things are woven together, and the bond is holy. The Buddha taught his own way of seeing it: when this is, that is; from the arising of this, that arises; when this ceases, that ceases. Nothing stands alone. A cup of tea holds rain, soil, hands and fire.
neighbors.difference: Marcus sees one reason running through a living cosmos and reveres it. The Buddha describes conditions arising together, without a creator behind them, and seeing it clearly helps free the mind.
neighbors.shared: nothing you hold got here alone.

neighbors.heading: no creature stands alone
neighbors.text: Today Marcus called the bond between all things holy. The Catechism says God wills the interdependence of creatures: the sun and the moon, the cedar and the small flower, the eagle and the sparrow. No creature is self-sufficient, it says; creatures exist in dependence on each other, to complete each other.
neighbors.difference: For Marcus, God runs through the universe as its reason. For Catholics, God creates the world and is not part of it, and the bond is holy because it comes from his hand.
neighbors.shared: handle each other with care; we're woven together.

neighbors.heading: hating no one
neighbors.text: Today Marcus said it's distinctly human to love even those who do wrong; they're kin who stumble. In the Gita, Krishna describes the one dear to him: hating no being, friendly and compassionate, free of I and mine, the same in pleasure and pain, forgiving.
neighbors.difference: Marcus loves wrongdoers because they're kin and err through ignorance. Krishna describes a devotee whose goodwill flows from devotion to God, present in every being.
neighbors.shared: they stumbled; you can still wish them well.

neighbors.heading: let sins cease
neighbors.text: Today Marcus said to love even people who do wrong. The Talmud tells of Beruriah, whose husband Rabbi Meir was praying that some troublemakers would die. She pointed to the psalm: let sins cease from the earth, not sinners. Pray that they turn back, she said. He did, and they did.
neighbors.difference: Marcus reasons from kinship and from wrong done in ignorance. Beruriah reads the psalm as a prayer, trusting God to turn a person to teshuvah, repentance.
neighbors.shared: hate the wrong; hope for the person.

items.lessonTitle: Not the whole life at once

neighbors.heading: sufficient unto the day
neighbors.text: Today Marcus told himself not to carry his whole life at once, just this piece. Jesus said it in the Sermon on the Mount: "Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof."
neighbors.difference: Marcus shrinks the moment by reason, asking what in it is really past bearing. Jesus grounds it in trust that the Father knows what his children need.
neighbors.shared: you only have to carry today.

neighbors.heading: not beyond its scope
neighbors.text: Today Marcus asked: what in this moment is actually past bearing? The Qur'an answers with a promise at the end of its longest surah: "Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope." Then comes a prayer asking not to be loaded with more than they can bear.
neighbors.difference: Marcus finds the strength in the size of the present moment. The Qur'an finds it in God's mercy, who measures each load and hears the prayer for a lighter one.
neighbors.shared: this piece is one you can hold.

neighbors.heading: instruct and bear
neighbors.text: Today Marcus wrote: people exist for one another; teach them, or bear with them. Catholics know those two doors from the spiritual works of mercy. Among them: instruct the ignorant, and bear wrongs patiently. Alongside them, the Church lists counseling, comforting and forgiving.
neighbors.difference: Marcus's reason is that people are made for each other, like hands. For Catholics, these are works of mercy done for Christ, who is served in the neighbor.
neighbors.shared: when you can't fix them, you can still carry them.

neighbors.heading: kiss their feet
neighbors.text: Today Marcus gave two doors with a difficult person: teach, or bear with them. Baba Farid, whose words are in the Sikh scripture, goes far down the second: if someone strikes you with fists, don't strike back. Go home, he says, and kiss their feet. Elsewhere Kabir says where there is forgiveness, God is there.
neighbors.difference: Marcus bears with people because they're made for one another. For Sikhs, forbearance and forgiveness are the way of one who sees the one Light in all.
neighbors.shared: bearing with someone is a kind of strength.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1378, Salok Farid; Ang 1372, Salok Kabir (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: rebuke, don't hate
neighbors.text: Today Marcus said: correct if you can, and if not, be kind. The Torah sets both in one verse: "Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thy heart; thou shalt surely rebuke thy neighbour." The next verse ends with love thy neighbour as thyself. And a psalm sings that God's tender mercies are over all his works.
neighbors.difference: Marcus points to gods who help even the wrong. In the Torah, rebuke is itself a commandment from God, and the rabbis warned it must never shame someone in public.
neighbors.shared: an honest word and a kind heart can go together.

neighbors.heading: five checks before you speak
neighbors.text: Today Marcus said correct by teaching, and if that fails, be kind. The Buddha gave his monks five checks before correcting someone: speak at the right time, speak what's true, speak gently, speak to help, and speak with a mind of goodwill.
neighbors.difference: Marcus grounds kindness in nature and the gods' generosity. The Buddha frames it as right speech, part of training the mind toward freedom from ill will.
neighbors.shared: say it true, say it kind, or let it wait.

neighbors.heading: no reward nor thanks
neighbors.text: Today Marcus said a good deed is already paid: an eye doesn't charge for seeing. The Qur'an describes the righteous feeding the needy, the orphan and the captive, saying: "We feed you, for the sake of Allah only. We wish for no reward nor thanks from you."
neighbors.difference: Marcus says the doing is the payment. For Muslims, the giver looks for no return from people because the reward is from God, who sees every kindness.
neighbors.shared: give without sending an invoice.

neighbors.heading: the work, not the fruit
neighbors.text: Today Marcus said if you've done good for others, you've already been rewarded. In the Gita, Krishna tells Arjuna: your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits. Don't let the fruit be your motive, he says, and don't cling to doing nothing either.
neighbors.difference: Marcus finds the reward inside the act, a limb helping its body. Krishna asks for action free of attachment, offered to God, as a path toward liberation.
neighbors.shared: the good you do is already enough.

neighbors.heading: remember their deeds
neighbors.text: Today Marcus copied an old rule: keep someone good from the past always in mind. Sikhs do this in Ardas, the prayer that closes their gatherings. It names the ten Gurus, then remembers Sikhs who gave their lives and kept their faith, and asks those present to think of their deeds.
neighbors.difference: Marcus remembers good people to steady his own choices. In Ardas, remembering is part of prayer to God, and the memory belongs to a whole community, not one person.
neighbors.shared: the good you remember walks with you.

neighbors.heading: a cloud of witnesses
neighbors.text: Today Marcus kept good people in mind, the way his notebook's first book thanks them one by one. A New Testament letter lists the faithful of old, then says: "seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight... and let us run with patience the race."
neighbors.difference: Marcus's good people are memories to learn from. For Christians, the witnesses point to Jesus, and the letter goes on to say to look to him most of all.
neighbors.shared: you run better when you remember who ran before you.

neighbors.heading: true, helpful, timely
neighbors.text: Today Marcus packed a two-gate rule: if it's not right, don't do it; if it's not true, don't say it. The Buddha described his own speech: he doesn't say what's untrue. Even what's true, he says only if it helps, and he knows the right time to say it, even when it's unwelcome.
neighbors.difference: Marcus treats a lie as a wrong against nature, which he calls truth. For the Buddha, right speech is a step on the eightfold path out of suffering.
neighbors.shared: a smaller true thing beats a big false one.

neighbors.heading: yea, yea; no, no
neighbors.text: Today Marcus said: if it's not true, don't say it. Jesus said it in the Sermon on the Mount: "But let your speech be yea, yea: no, no: and that which is over and above these, is of evil." The Catechism adds that truthfulness keeps discretion too: not every true thing must be said.
neighbors.difference: For Marcus, truth is bound up with reason and nature itself. For Catholics, truthfulness honors God, who is truth, and Jesus, who called himself the truth.
neighbors.shared: say what's true, and say it kindly.
neighbors.sources: Matthew 5:37 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 2469, 2489 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: your own dharma
neighbors.text: Today Panaetius taught that each person has their own nature, and a fitting duty in their own role. Hindus hear the Gita: better your own dharma done imperfectly than another's done well. Krishna says it to a warrior who wishes he could walk away from his part.
neighbors.difference: Panaetius's duties fit a person's nature and role in a city. In the Gita, dharma belongs to a sacred order, and doing it as an offering to God becomes a path to freedom.
neighbors.shared: you don't have to live anyone else's life.

neighbors.heading: not yours to finish
neighbors.text: Today Panaetius made a path ordinary people could walk: do the fitting thing today, without being a sage. A rabbi in the Mishnah said it like this: the day is short and the work is great. It isn't your duty to finish the work, but you aren't free to stop doing it.
neighbors.difference: Panaetius's path leads toward virtue for a citizen. Rabbi Tarfon's work is Torah and the commandments, done before God, who rewards the worker.
neighbors.shared: you don't have to be finished to be faithful.
neighbors.sources: Pirkei Avot 2:15–16, numbered 2:20–21 in some editions (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: learned to be content
neighbors.text: Today Epicurus said plain bread tastes like a feast to the hungry, and wanting little makes you hard to frighten. Paul wrote from a hard place: "I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content." He knew hunger and plenty, he says, and learned how to live with both.
neighbors.difference: Epicurus's contentment is a wise training of desire for a calm life. Paul says his strength for any state comes from Christ.
neighbors.shared: less is easier to carry.

neighbors.heading: richness of the soul
neighbors.text: Today Epicurus said needs that are natural are easy to meet, and a person content with bread and water can't be threatened much. The Prophet Muhammad said it in one line: richness isn't having many possessions; real richness is the richness of the soul.
neighbors.difference: For Epicurus, wanting little brings a calm life here, with nothing after it. For Muslims, contentment is gratitude to God, who provides, and is part of faith.
neighbors.shared: enough feels like a feast when you notice it.

neighbors.heading: a treasure found
neighbors.text: Today Epicurus said friendship is the greatest thing wisdom gives for a happy life. Catholics keep a book of wisdom that agrees: "A faithful friend is a strong defence: and he that hath found him, hath found a treasure." It goes on to call a faithful friend the medicine of life.
neighbors.difference: Epicurus prizes friendship for a calm, unafraid life here. The same Catholic book says those who fear the Lord will find such a friend, so friendship is also a gift from God.
neighbors.shared: a faithful friend is worth more than gold.

neighbors.heading: friends who walk with me
neighbors.text: Today Epicurus said it's our trust that friends would help that takes the fear out of life. Guru Nanak names the friends who matter: they alone are my friends who walk with me as I go, and stand by me where the account is called.
neighbors.difference: Epicurus's friends ease life here, with nothing after. For Guru Nanak, the truest friends stay with you before God, beyond this life.
neighbors.shared: the friend who stays when it's hard is the real one.

neighbors.heading: a wheel that turns
neighbors.text: Today Philosophy told Boethius that Fortune's only constancy is change. The Talmud has the same wheel. Rabbi Hiyya told his wife to be quick to give bread to a poor man, so that their own children would be treated the same way. Poverty, he said, is a wheel that turns in the world.
neighbors.difference: Boethius learns to hold good fortune loosely. Rabbi Hiyya draws a duty from the turning wheel: give now, because anyone can end up on the other side.
neighbors.shared: the wheel turns, so be kind on the way up.

neighbors.heading: eight winds
neighbors.text: Today Fortune told Boethius she lends everything and takes it back. The Buddha named eight worldly conditions, later called the eight winds: gain and loss, fame and disrepute, praise and blame, pleasure and pain. They come to everyone, he said. The difference is whether you see that they don't last, and don't let them take over your mind.
neighbors.difference: Boethius's consolation turns to a good the wheel can't reach, and finally to God. The Buddha's leads further, to seeing everything as impermanent and letting go of clinging.
neighbors.shared: the winds blow on everyone; you don't have to blow away.

neighbors.heading: return, content
neighbors.text: Today Marcus pictured ending life like a ripe olive falling, blessing the tree that grew it. The Qur'an speaks of an ending at peace too: "But ah! thou soul at peace! Return unto thy Lord, content in His good pleasure!" The soul goes back content, and welcome.
neighbors.difference: Marcus imagines returning to nature, grateful, without a promise of what comes next. The Qur'an speaks of the soul returning to God and being invited into His Garden.
neighbors.shared: a life can end in thanks, not only in loss.

neighbors.heading: the ripe fruit from the vine
neighbors.text: Today Marcus said to end like a ripe olive, falling in its season. Hindus have a ripe-fruit picture in an old Vedic mantra, the Mahamrityunjaya, prayed to Shiva: like a ripe cucumber freed from its vine, may I be freed from death, not from the deathless.
neighbors.difference: Marcus's olive falls back into nature, giving thanks. The mantra asks God for liberation: release from death into what never dies.
neighbors.shared: in its season, the fruit lets go.

neighbors.heading: the ambrosial hours
neighbors.text: Today the Stoic morning was a two-minute start: preview, principle, intention. Sikhs have a morning practice too. Guru Nanak's Japji says: in the amrit vela, the ambrosial hours before dawn, chant the True Name and reflect on its greatness. Guru Ram Das describes a Sikh rising early to bathe and meditate on the Name.
neighbors.difference: The Stoic morning readies the mind for the people and work ahead. Amrit vela is time with God's Name, the day's first meeting with the One.
neighbors.shared: meet the morning before it meets you.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 2, Japji 4; Ang 305 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: in the morning
neighbors.text: Today Marcus began his mornings with a preview, a principle and an intention. The psalmist began his with prayer: "My voice shalt thou hear in the morning, O LORD; in the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee, and will look up." Christians have long kept a morning prayer before the day begins.
neighbors.difference: Marcus talks to himself to get ready. The psalmist talks to God, and the morning is a turning toward him before anything else.
neighbors.shared: the first minutes can set the whole day.

neighbors.heading: the real driver
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said the greatest cure for anger is delay. The Dhammapada has a picture for that moment: "He who holds back rising anger like a rolling chariot, him I call a real driver; other people are but holding the reins."
neighbors.difference: Seneca delays so the judgment under the anger can be checked. The Buddha teaches letting anger go as part of freeing the mind from hatred altogether.
neighbors.shared: the pause is where you take the reins.

neighbors.heading: slow to anger
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said: feel the jolt, delay the reply. A New Testament letter has the same order: "let every man be swift to hear, but slow to speak, and slow to anger." For anger, it says, does not work the justice of God. Catholics count meekness among the beatitudes.
neighbors.difference: Seneca's delay serves a calm, reasoning mind. For Catholics, slowness to anger is part of a life lived toward God, and grace helps where effort runs out.
neighbors.shared: listen first; the reply can wait.

neighbors.heading: twenty-four teachers
neighbors.text: Today the chain of Stoic wisdom began with an enslaved man nobody would have bet on. Hindus tell of a wandering sage, Dattatreya, who tells a king he had twenty-four teachers: the earth, the wind, a python, a moth, a child, even a woman of the town named Pingala. Each taught him something.
neighbors.difference: Marcus learned from Epictetus through notes and a friend's copy. Dattatreya learns from the whole world, and each lesson points toward freedom and the Self.
neighbors.shared: teachers turn up where you least expect them.

neighbors.heading: learn from everyone
neighbors.text: Today the teacher was a freed slave, and an emperor thanked him. The Mishnah asks: who is wise? Ben Zoma answers: the one who learns from every person. He reads a psalm for proof: from all my teachers I have gained understanding.
neighbors.difference: Marcus honors one unlikely teacher. Ben Zoma makes learning from anyone a rule of wisdom, rooted in Torah.
neighbors.shared: the person nobody bet on may be your teacher.

neighbors.heading: the good that I would
neighbors.text: Today the Stoics admitted their method didn't always work, even on them. Paul was honest the same way: "For the good that I would I do not: but the evil which I would not, that I do." A teacher of the faith, writing honestly about falling short.
neighbors.difference: The Stoics answer falling short by returning to practice. Paul answers it by pointing beyond himself to God's grace in Jesus.
neighbors.shared: saying "it didn't work" is part of the practice.

neighbors.heading: the best who fall
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus asked to be shown a Stoic, and implied he hadn't seen one. Muslims keep a saying of the Prophet that is just as honest: every child of Adam errs, and the best of those who err are those who turn back.
neighbors.difference: The Stoics turn back to their practice. In Islam, turning back is tawbah, repentance to God, who the Qur'an says loves those who turn to him.
neighbors.shared: nobody does it perfectly; the turning back counts.
neighbors.sources: Sunan al-Tirmidhi 2499; Sunan Ibn Majah 4251 (paraphrase) · Qur'an 2:222 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: overcome evil by good
neighbors.text: Today an old verse said hatred never ends by hatred, only by love. Catholics hear Jesus say something close on a mountainside: "Love your enemies: do good to them that hate you: and pray for them that persecute and calumniate you." Paul adds a short rule of his own: "Be not overcome by evil, but overcome evil by good."
neighbors.difference: The Dhammapada calls this an old law, simply how hatred works, like fire. For Catholics, loving an enemy imitates God the Father, who sends rain on the just and the unjust, and it is made possible by grace.
neighbors.shared: hatred stops where someone refuses to pass it on.

neighbors.heading: no one is my enemy
neighbors.text: Today an old verse said hatred ends only by love. Sikhs sing something close. Guru Arjan wrote that since he found the company of the holy, no one is his enemy and no one a stranger; he gets along with all. And Baba Farid, whose verses sit in the Guru Granth Sahib, says: answer evil with good, and don't let anger fill your mind.
neighbors.difference: The Dhammapada roots this in how the mind works. For Sikhs, no one is finally an enemy because the one God's light shines in every person.
neighbors.shared: anger set down is lighter than anger carried.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Raag Kaanraa, Guru Arjan (paraphrase) · Guru Granth Sahib, Salok Farid (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: not in our hands
neighbors.text: Today Job's friends explained his suffering, and the book says they were wrong. Jewish sages kept that humility. In Pirkei Avot, Rabbi Yannai says, in paraphrase: it is not in our hands to explain why the wicked are at ease or why the righteous suffer. And when a sick rabbi was asked if his sufferings were dear to him, he said: neither they nor their reward.
neighbors.difference: Job is a story where God himself rebukes the explainers. The rabbis kept more than one voice: some did look for reasons, even calling some pain "sufferings of love", and the Talmud sets those beside the humbler answer.
neighbors.shared: not every pain needs an explanation; sometimes it needs a hand.
neighbors.sources: Pirkei Avot 4:15 (4:19 in some editions) (paraphrase) · Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 5a-5b (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: not all from past deeds
neighbors.text: Today Job's friends insisted his suffering must be deserved. A man named Sivaka once asked the Buddha something close: is everything we feel caused by past deeds? No, the Buddha said, in paraphrase. Some pain comes from the body, some from the change of seasons, from carelessness, from violence done to us, and some from past action. To say it's all past deeds goes too far.
neighbors.difference: Job's question is about a just God and an innocent man. The Buddha speaks of no God who judges; karma is real for him, just not the whole explanation of every pain.
neighbors.shared: not every wound is a verdict on the one who carries it.

neighbors.heading: this is mercy
neighbors.text: Today Jesus wept at his friend's tomb, and the people said, see how he loved him. Muslims remember a father's tears too. When the Prophet's ﷺ baby son Ibrahim was dying, his eyes filled, and a companion was surprised. The Prophet said, in paraphrase: this is mercy. The eyes weep and the heart grieves, and we say only what pleases our Lord.
neighbors.difference: For Christians, Jesus is the Son of God made flesh, so these are God's own tears. For Muslims, Muhammad ﷺ is a human messenger, not divine, and his tears show the mercy God places in human hearts.
neighbors.shared: tears for someone you love are not a lack of faith.

neighbors.heading: Rama weeps in the forest
neighbors.text: Today Jesus wept for Lazarus, and his tears showed his love. Hindus tell of tears like that in the Ramayana. When Sita is taken, Rama searches the forest weeping, asking the trees, the rivers and the deer whether they have seen her. Many Hindus honor Rama as an avatar of Vishnu, and the epic doesn't hide his grief.
neighbors.difference: Christians speak of one incarnation, Jesus, who weeps and then calls Lazarus out of the tomb. Hindus speak of Vishnu coming down in many forms; some read Rama's grief as fully human, others as divine play.
neighbors.shared: grief is how love looks when someone is missing.

neighbors.heading: a bow made of patience
neighbors.text: Today Jacob lost his son and chose a beautiful patience, sabr. The same word lives in the Sikh scripture. Baba Farid, whose verses sit in the Guru Granth Sahib, says, in paraphrase: let patience be your bow, patience your bowstring, patience your arrow, and the Creator will not let it miss.
neighbors.difference: In the Quran, Jacob is a prophet whose patience carries his grief to God, and the story gives Joseph back. Farid's patience aims at God himself: its hope is nearness to the Creator.
neighbors.shared: patience isn't giving up; it's holding steady while you hope.

neighbors.heading: patient in tribulation
neighbors.text: Today Jacob grieved for Joseph with a beautiful patience. Christians know the same father from Genesis, where his children try to comfort him, "but he refused to be comforted." And Paul, writing to Christians in Rome, asks for a patience that still hopes: "Rejoicing in hope; patient in tribulation; continuing instant in prayer."
neighbors.difference: In the Quran, Jacob names his patience beautiful and takes his grief to God alone. In Genesis, he refuses comfort outright, and Christians hear Paul's patience as hope fixed on Christ.
neighbors.shared: you can grieve hard and still keep a door open to hope.

neighbors.heading: self is the lord of self
neighbors.text: Today Frankl said one freedom stays when everything else is taken: the stance you choose. An old Buddhist verse points to the same inner ground: "Self is the lord of self, who else could be the lord?" Many Buddhists train it in small ways, noticing anger or fear as it rises and letting it pass before it acts.
neighbors.difference: Frankl found meaning by choosing a stance toward suffering. Buddhist practice aims at seeing through the craving behind suffering, and it also teaches that no fixed, lasting self lies underneath.
neighbors.shared: what happens to you isn't all that happens in you.

neighbors.heading: a martyr of charity
neighbors.text: Today Frankl said one freedom can't be taken: how you meet what happens. Catholics remember a priest who used that freedom in Auschwitz. Maximilian Kolbe, a Franciscan prisoner, stepped forward to die in place of a man condemned to starve, a husband and father. The Church reads his choice by Jesus' words: "Greater love than this no man hath, that a man lay down his life for his friends."
neighbors.difference: Frankl, a psychiatrist, writes of a freedom every person has, whatever they believe. Catholics see Kolbe's choice as grace: Christ's own love at work in him, given for someone else.
neighbors.shared: even with almost everything taken, love can still choose.
neighbors.sources: John 15:13 (Douay-Rheims) · St. Maximilian Kolbe, honored by the Church as a martyr of charity (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: their pain as your own
neighbors.text: Today's practice said: this is hard, and others feel this too. The Bhagavad Gita turns that thought outward. Krishna says, in paraphrase, that the highest yogi is the one who, by the likeness of their own self, sees the joy and the pain of every being as their own. Your own hurt becomes a window onto everyone's.
neighbors.difference: Neff's practice is kindness turned inward, grounded in psychology. In the Gita the likeness runs deeper: Krishna teaches seeing the Self in every being, so another's pain truly concerns you.
neighbors.shared: you're not the only one who hurts, and neither are they.

neighbors.heading: you know the heart of a stranger
neighbors.text: Today's practice said: this is hard, and others feel this too. The Torah builds a law on that same knowing: "And a stranger shalt thou not oppress; for ye know the heart of a stranger, seeing ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." Remembered pain, the verse says, is how you understand someone else's.
neighbors.difference: Neff's common humanity is something you remind yourself of, to be kinder to yourself. The Torah makes it a commandment, rooted in a whole people's memory of Egypt, and points it at the stranger.
neighbors.shared: your own hard days can make you gentler with everyone else's.

neighbors.heading: by whose stripes
neighbors.text: Today an old myth said a healer's own wound can help them understand. Christians say something like it about Jesus himself. A letter to the Hebrews says: "For in that he himself hath suffered being tempted, he is able to succour them that are tempted." And Peter's letter speaks of Christ, "by whose stripes ye were healed."
neighbors.difference: In the myth and in modern care, a hurt person helps others by understanding them. Christians believe Christ's wounds do more than understand: they heal and save, as God's own self-giving.
neighbors.shared: the ones who've been hurt often know best how to sit with hurt.

neighbors.heading: once an orphan
neighbors.text: Today an old myth said a healer's own wound can help them heal others. The Quran speaks to the Prophet ﷺ in that spirit. It reminds him, in paraphrase: did God not find you an orphan and give you shelter? Did He not find you in need and provide? So do not be harsh with the orphan, and do not turn away the one who asks.
neighbors.difference: The wounded-healer idea says hurt can deepen understanding. The Quran ties it to gratitude to God: you were sheltered, so shelter others, as a command, not only a gift of empathy.
neighbors.shared: what was once done for you can become what you do for others.

neighbors.heading: sow in tears
neighbors.text: Today Seneca looked at a burned city and said it could rise again. Catholics pray a psalm about a people coming home from ruin: "They that sow in tears shall reap in joy." And the Easter Vigil begins in darkness: a new fire is lit, and its light is carried into the dark church.
neighbors.difference: Seneca's hope rests on nature's cycles and a steady mind: what falls can be rebuilt. For Catholics, hope rests on God, who raised Christ from the tomb and can bring life out of ruin.
neighbors.shared: ruin is real, and so is rebuilding.
neighbors.sources: Psalm 125:5 (Douay-Rheims; Psalm 126:5 in many Bibles) · the Easter Vigil (described)

neighbors.heading: chardi kala
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said a burned city can rise again. Sikhs have a word for a spirit that keeps rising: chardi kala. Their daily prayer, the Ardas, remembers Sikhs who suffered terribly for their faith, and still it closes: Nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhane sarbat da bhala. With the Name, spirits rise; in your will, may all be well.
neighbors.difference: Seneca steadies himself with reason: expect loss, then rebuild. For Sikhs, chardi kala isn't only a strong mind; it's kept by remembering God's Name and accepting God's will.
neighbors.shared: a spirit can stay high even while the walls are down.
neighbors.sources: Ardas, the Sikh daily prayer (paraphrase of the closing line)

neighbors.heading: plant the sapling first
neighbors.text: Today Montaigne hoped death would find him planting cabbages. A Jewish sage, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, gave planting its place even at the end of days. In paraphrase: if you are holding a sapling and someone cries that the Messiah has come, plant the sapling first, then go out to greet him.
neighbors.difference: Montaigne wants to meet his own death unbothered, busy with ordinary work. The rabbi's saying looks to the world's future and God's promise: even then, the work in your hands still matters.
neighbors.shared: keep planting; the ordinary work of today is never wasted.

neighbors.heading: today the effort
neighbors.text: Today Montaigne said that to philosophize is to learn to die. A Buddhist verse, the teaching of One Fine Night, says it in its own way, in paraphrase: don't chase the past or pine for the future; see clearly what is here now. Do today what needs doing. Who knows? Death may come tomorrow.
neighbors.difference: Montaigne wants death to be familiar so it stops ruling him. In the Buddha's verse, remembering death fuels the effort to see clearly and, in time, to be free of the round of rebirth.
neighbors.shared: today is the one day you can be sure of.

neighbors.heading: as a traveler
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha praised the monk who remembers death within a single breath. Muslims keep a saying close to that. The Prophet ﷺ told Ibn Umar, in paraphrase: be in this world as a stranger or a traveler. And Ibn Umar would add: in the evening, don't count on morning; in the morning, don't count on evening. Take from your health for your sickness.
neighbors.difference: For the Buddha, remembering death sharpens practice toward the deathless. For Muslims, it is preparation to meet God, who will weigh each life, with hope in God's mercy.
neighbors.shared: an honest look at the end makes this hour count.

neighbors.heading: what you remember at the end
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha asked his monks to remember death with every breath. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says, in paraphrase: whatever a person remembers as they leave the body, to that they go. So remember me at all times, and do your duty. The last moment is shaped by all the ordinary ones before it.
neighbors.difference: The Buddha's monks remember death to stay awake and reach the deathless, teaching no lasting self that passes on. In the Gita, the self goes on, and remembering Krishna carries it to him.
neighbors.shared: how we spend ordinary moments shapes the last one.

neighbors.heading: sing, don't weep
neighbors.text: Today the mourner's Kaddish praised God and never named death. Sikhs keep something close. A poem in the Guru Granth Sahib, the Sadd, remembers Guru Amar Das asking, near his end, that no one weep for him, but that they sing God's praise and hear God's word instead. Sikh funerals often include kirtan, hymns sung to the one who gave life.
neighbors.difference: The Kaddish keeps tears and praise together, said by mourners in a gathered quorum. Sikh teaching speaks of death as the soul going home to God, and the Guru asks that the praise come without weeping.
neighbors.shared: praise can still be sung with a broken heart.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Raag Ramkali, Sadd (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: blessed be the name
neighbors.text: Today the Kaddish praised God beside a grave. In the old Anglican prayer book, Christians walk to the grave praising too. The burial service opens with sentences from Scripture, among them Job's: "The Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away; blessed be the Name of the Lord." Grief and praise walk in together.
neighbors.difference: The mourner's Kaddish never mentions death. The Christian service names it plainly, and its first words are Jesus' own, "I am the resurrection and the life", so its praise leans on the hope of rising in Christ.
neighbors.shared: praising God at a grave is faith said out loud.
neighbors.sources: Book of Common Prayer 1662, The Order for the Burial of the Dead · Job 1:21 · John 11:25

neighbors.heading: Ananda at the door
neighbors.text: Today the Prophet ﷺ wept for his son and called the tears mercy. Buddhists remember tears near the end of the Buddha's life. His attendant Ananda went inside, leaned on the doorpost and wept. The Buddha called him and said, in paraphrase: enough, Ananda, don't grieve. Haven't I told you that all we hold dear must change? Then he praised Ananda's years of loving care.
neighbors.difference: In the hadith, tears are called mercy, held within what pleases God. The Buddha comforts Ananda by pointing to impermanence, a truth to see through, so that grief can loosen its grip.
neighbors.shared: even the closest followers wept, and were met with tenderness.

neighbors.heading: a sword through her soul
neighbors.text: Today the Prophet ﷺ wept for his son and called the tears mercy. Catholics keep a mother's grief close. When Mary brought her baby to the Temple, Simeon told her: "And thy own soul a sword shall pierce." An old hymn, the Stabat Mater, pictures her at the cross, weeping, close to her Son to the last. Catholics honor her as Our Lady of Sorrows.
neighbors.difference: In the hadith, a prophet weeps as a father and says only what pleases God. Catholics see Mary's sorrow joined to her Son's suffering for the world, and many ask her prayers in their own grief.
neighbors.shared: a parent's grief is love with nowhere left to go.

neighbors.heading: rice and water for the ancestors
neighbors.text: Today families swept their ancestors' tombs at Qingming. Hindu families keep a season for this too: Pitru Paksha, the fortnight of the ancestors. In shraddha rites they offer pinda, balls of rice, with water and sesame, and speak the names of parents and grandparents. An old Upanishad tells students leaving their teacher: do not neglect your duties to the gods and to the ancestors.
neighbors.difference: At Qingming, care is shown at the grave itself. Hindus usually cremate, so there's no grave to sweep; shraddha offerings, believed to nourish the ancestors, are made at home or beside a holy river.
neighbors.shared: the people who came before you are still worth tending.
neighbors.sources: Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11 (paraphrase) · shraddha and Pitru Paksha customs (described)

neighbors.heading: a candle for the year's turn
neighbors.text: Today families swept their ancestors' tombs. Jewish families keep a day too: the yahrzeit, the anniversary of a death. A candle burns through the day, and Kaddish is said. Many link the flame to a proverb: "The spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD." At the grave, visitors often leave a small stone to show someone came.
neighbors.difference: At Qingming, many families set out food and paper offerings the dead might need. Jewish practice offers nothing to the dead; the living pray to God, give charity and study in their memory.
neighbors.shared: remembering is done with hands: a stone, a flame, a cleared grave.

neighbors.heading: rich toward God
neighbors.text: Today a hospice nurse said the dying often wish they hadn't worked so hard. Jesus told a story about that. A rich man plans bigger barns and a long, easy rest. Then God says: "Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?"
neighbors.difference: Ware's regrets are about living true to yourself and the people you love. Jesus' story points past that, to being "rich toward God": a life measured by God, not only by your own heart.
neighbors.shared: the end shows what mattered; it's kinder to look now.

neighbors.heading: until ye come to the graves
neighbors.text: Today a hospice nurse heard the dying wish they had lived less for other people's expectations. A short chapter of the Quran says it in two lines: "Rivalry in worldly increase distracteth you until ye come to the graves." Another verse pictures someone at death asking, in paraphrase: Lord, give me a little more time, and I would give in charity and do good.
neighbors.difference: Ware's regrets look back over a life, measured by its own truest wishes. The Quran adds an accounting before God, and asks for the change now, while there's still time to give.
neighbors.shared: you don't have to wait for the end to see what matters.

neighbors.heading: the communion of saints
neighbors.text: Today grief researchers said many people keep a bond with those who've died. Catholics say that bond is real. In the Creed they profess "the communion of saints": the living and the dead, one family in Christ. They pray for their dead by name, and an old book says: "It is therefore a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead."
neighbors.difference: Researchers describe the bond as memory and meaning carried by the mourner, without saying where the dead are. Catholics believe the dead live in God, and that prayer truly reaches and helps them.
neighbors.shared: love doesn't have to end where a life does.
neighbors.sources: Apostles' Creed · 2 Machabees 12:46 (Douay-Rheims; 2 Maccabees in many Bibles)

neighbors.heading: named in every Ardas
neighbors.text: Today grief researchers said keeping a bond with the dead can be healthy. Sikhs remember their dead aloud. The Ardas, the prayer that closes Sikh gatherings, names the Gurus and recalls the Sikhs who gave their lives for their faith. When someone dies, families often hold a reading of the whole Guru Granth Sahib, with a prayer that the soul rest at God's feet.
neighbors.difference: Researchers speak of a bond kept inside the mourner. Sikh teaching sees the soul returning to God, and the Gurus turned away from rites meant to feed or serve the dead; remembrance is praise, not offering.
neighbors.shared: the ones we've lost can still be named with love.
neighbors.sources: Ardas, the Sikh prayer (described) · Sahaj Path and Ardas at a Sikh funeral (described)

neighbors.heading: pursue peace
neighbors.text: Today the texts said make peace before the sun goes down. Hillel put it as a calling: be like the disciples of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace. The rabbis told how Aaron did it. When two people quarreled, he would sit with each one and say, the other is heartbroken over this, until they met and embraced.
neighbors.difference: The lesson's texts ask you to mend your own quarrels. Aaron, in the rabbis' telling, went further: he chased peace between other people, even, in that telling, shading the truth a little.
neighbors.shared: peace usually needs someone to go first.
neighbors.sources: Pirkei Avot 1:12 (paraphrase) · Avot de-Rabbi Natan, version A, 12 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: their quarrels cease
neighbors.text: Today the texts said make peace before the sun goes down. An old Buddhist verse gives its own reason: "The world does not know that we must all come to an end here; but those who know it, their quarrels cease at once." Remember the ending, the verse says, and the fight shrinks.
neighbors.difference: The lesson's texts ask for mending before God and the community. The Dhammapada speaks of no God here; quarrels end because death, seen clearly, makes them look small.
neighbors.shared: life is short enough that most quarrels aren't worth keeping.

neighbors.heading: your body has a right
neighbors.text: Today's lesson thanked the body that carried you here. Muslims remember a word from the Prophet ﷺ about this. When a young companion fasted every day and prayed all night, the Prophet told him, in paraphrase: fast some days and eat on others; pray, and sleep too. Your body has a right over you, and your eyes have a right over you.
neighbors.difference: The psalm praises the body as wonderfully made. Islam also frames it as a trust from God with rights of its own, so resting, eating and caring for it can be part of worship.
neighbors.shared: caring for your body is a kind of thank-you.

neighbors.heading: the first tool of dharma
neighbors.text: Today's lesson thanked the body that carried you here. A line from the Sanskrit poet Kalidasa is still quoted in Hindu homes: the body is the very first means of living dharma. In his poem, it's said to the goddess Parvati as she wears herself out with hard austerities: take care, the body is what makes the practice possible.
neighbors.difference: The psalm and the blessing thank God for a body that is made and fragile. Many Hindus see the body as a vehicle for the self, which is not the body: honored as the chariot, not the rider.
neighbors.shared: the body you have is the one that carries your practice.

neighbors.heading: the true company
neighbors.text: Today Aristotle said the best friends are good, and wish each other good. Sikhs prize that kind of company: the sangat. Guru Nanak asks, in paraphrase, how is the true company known? It's where the one Name is spoken. Sikhs gather in it to sing, serve and eat together, and the company itself helps make them good.
neighbors.difference: Aristotle's best friendships are rare, between people already good and alike. The sangat is open to anyone who comes, and gathers around God's Name rather than around two people.
neighbors.shared: the people you sit with help shape who you become.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: provoke unto love
neighbors.text: Today Aristotle said the best friends wish each other good for the other's own sake. An early Christian letter asks a whole church for that: "And let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works." And Jesus tells his disciples: "I have called you friends."
neighbors.difference: Aristotle saves the highest friendship for a few equals in goodness. Christians call fellow believers, even strangers, brothers and sisters, and see their deepest friendship as one Christ offers first.
neighbors.shared: a good friend makes you want to be good.

neighbors.heading: the whole of the path
neighbors.text: Today Ruth refused to leave Naomi: where you die, I will die. Buddhists honor faithful friendship too. Ananda once said good friends are half of the spiritual life. Not half, the Buddha answered, in paraphrase: good friendship is the whole of it. Elsewhere he says a true friend doesn't abandon you when you fall on hard times.
neighbors.difference: Ruth binds herself for life to Naomi's people and God. The Buddha's good friend is a companion on the path toward freedom, and Buddhists also teach not to cling, even to those dearest.
neighbors.shared: staying with someone through the hard years is a kind of love.
neighbors.sources: Samyutta Nikaya 45.2, Upaddha Sutta (paraphrase) · Digha Nikaya 31, Sigalovada Sutta (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: behold thy mother
neighbors.text: Today Ruth chose Naomi: thy people shall be my people. Catholics keep a scene like it at the cross. Jesus, dying, sees his mother and the disciple he loved, and joins them: "Woman, behold thy son." Then: "Behold thy mother." And from that hour, the disciple "took her to his own."
neighbors.difference: Ruth chooses Naomi herself, at a cost to her own future. In John, Jesus gives the two to each other, and Catholics read it as Mary given as mother to every disciple.
neighbors.shared: family can be chosen, and kept, in the hardest hour.

neighbors.heading: a leaf, a flower
neighbors.text: Today Thérèse offered small things with great love, like strewing flowers. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says something close, in paraphrase: whoever offers me with love a leaf, a flower, a fruit or a little water, I accept it, offered from a devoted heart. In many Hindu homes, the daily offering is just that small.
neighbors.difference: Thérèse offers her small acts to Jesus, trusting his arms to lift her. Krishna speaks as the Lord receiving the gift himself; in bhakti, the love behind the offering is what reaches him.
neighbors.shared: nothing is too small when it's given with love.

neighbors.heading: much or little
neighbors.text: Today Thérèse said small acts of love count. The Talmud has a short line Jews still quote, in paraphrase: one may do much or one may do little, as long as the heart is turned toward Heaven. And Pirkei Avot asks for the same care with a light commandment as with a weighty one, since we can't know their reward.
neighbors.difference: Thérèse's little way is love offered to Jesus and lifted by grace. Jewish teaching ties the small deed to the mitzvot, the commandments, done faithfully for God, whose weight only God knows.
neighbors.shared: a small thing done with your whole heart is not small.

neighbors.heading: as a hen gathereth
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha asked for love as fierce as a mother's for her only child, spread to all beings. Jesus reaches for a mother's picture too. Grieving over a city that turned him away, he says: "how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings."
neighbors.difference: In the Metta Sutta, a person grows boundless love step by step, without speaking of God. Jesus speaks of his own love, and Christians see in it God's love reaching out, even to those who turn away.
neighbors.shared: the fiercest love we know points to a wider one.

neighbors.heading: more merciful than a mother
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha pictured a mother guarding her only child. The Prophet ﷺ once pointed to a mother too. Among captives, a woman searched desperately, found her baby and held it to nurse. The Prophet asked, in paraphrase: would she ever throw her child into a fire? No, they said. God is more merciful to His servants than she is to her child.
neighbors.difference: The Metta Sutta asks people to grow a mother's love toward all beings. The hadith speaks of God's own mercy, greater than any mother's; Muslims see human mercy as a small share of it.
neighbors.shared: a mother's love is the closest picture we have of something bigger.

neighbors.heading: a lotus in the water
neighbors.text: Today equanimity meant loving without clinging. Sikhs have a picture for it. In the Sidh Gosht, a conversation with yogis, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase: the lotus lives in the water and stays untouched; the duck swims the stream and stays dry. Live in the world like that, with your mind fixed on the Word.
neighbors.difference: Buddhist equanimity rests on seeing that beings own their deeds. Guru Nanak's loose grip comes from holding on to God's Name instead, and he asks for it inside family life, not apart from it.
neighbors.shared: you can hold people close without holding on too tight.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Raag Ramkali, Sidh Gosht (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: holy indifference
neighbors.text: Today equanimity meant an even heart, close enough to love, loose enough not to grab. Catholics in the Jesuit tradition call something like it indifference. St. Ignatius writes, in paraphrase: don't prefer health to sickness, riches to poverty, honor to dishonor, a long life to a short one; want only what best leads to the end we're made for, God.
neighbors.difference: Buddhist equanimity steadies love toward all beings, seeing that each owns their deeds. Ignatian indifference loosens the grip on everything so the heart is free to choose God; it isn't coldness toward people.
neighbors.shared: a loose grip can make room for a bigger love.
neighbors.sources: St. Ignatius of Loyola, Spiritual Exercises, Principle and Foundation (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: betrothed every morning
neighbors.text: Today love was a daily choice, not only a feeling. On weekday mornings, Jews who wind tefillin around a finger say a vow from Hosea, God speaking to Israel like a groom: "I will betroth thee unto Me in righteousness, and in justice, and in lovingkindness, and in compassion." The same promise, renewed each morning.
neighbors.difference: Fromm and Paul describe love between people as an art practiced daily. Hosea's betrothal is God's covenant with a people; the morning vow binds a person to God, and couples can borrow its shape.
neighbors.shared: love gets chosen again, morning by morning.

neighbors.heading: in this life and the next
neighbors.text: Today love was a daily choice. The Buddha once met an old couple, Nakula's father and mother. The husband said, in paraphrase: since she came to me as a girl, I've never been unfaithful to her, even in thought. Both hoped to be together in lives to come. The Buddha said: if you match in faith, goodness, generosity and wisdom, you will.
neighbors.difference: Fromm treats love as an art of living for this life. In the Buddha's answer, a couple's shared goodness can carry their bond into lives to come, through karma and rebirth.
neighbors.shared: love lasts when it's grown together, day after day.

neighbors.heading: the wing of mercy
neighbors.text: Today honor meant actions, with honest limits. The Quran asks for both. In paraphrase: be kind to your parents; when they grow old, don't even sigh at them in irritation, and lower to them the wing of humility, out of mercy. But if they press you to worship anything beside God, don't obey that, and still keep them company kindly in this world.
neighbors.difference: Exodus and the rabbis spell honor out as deeds. The Quran sets kindness to parents right beside worshipping God alone, and names its one limit plainly: no obeying them against God.
neighbors.shared: you can honor a parent and still keep your own conscience.

neighbors.heading: let your mother be a god to you
neighbors.text: Today honor meant care and respect, even when it's hard. An old Upanishad tells students leaving their teacher: let your mother be a god to you; let your father be a god to you. And Hindus tell of young Prahlada, who stayed respectful to his father, a cruel king, yet would not give up his love for Vishnu.
neighbors.difference: Exodus asks for honor, and Confucius for respect. The Upanishad asks that parents be treated as divine, while Prahlada's story shows even that honor stops short of turning from God.
neighbors.shared: honoring parents doesn't mean pretending they're perfect.
neighbors.sources: Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11 (paraphrase) · Bhagavata Purana, book 7, Prahlada (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: seva
neighbors.text: Today drops of water filled a pot, a little at a time. Sikhs live this in seva, selfless service. At the gurdwara, people wipe shoes, wash dishes and roll rotis for the langar, the free kitchen where anyone can eat. Guru Arjan wrote, in paraphrase, that one who serves without wanting anything back reaches the Lord.
neighbors.difference: The Dhammapada gathers good drop by drop toward a purer mind. Seva is offered to God through serving people, done side by side in a shared kitchen, without counting.
neighbors.shared: a plate washed for a stranger still counts.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan (paraphrase) · langar and seva (described)

neighbors.heading: two mites
neighbors.text: Today small kindnesses added up like drops in a pot. Jesus once watched people giving at the Temple. Rich people gave much. "And there came a certain poor widow, and she threw in two mites." He tells his friends: "this poor widow hath cast more in, than all they which have cast into the treasury."
neighbors.difference: The Dhammapada counts small goods adding up over time. Jesus measures the widow by what it cost her, all she had, given to God, not by the size of the coin.
neighbors.shared: a gift is measured by the heart, not the amount.

neighbors.heading: a blessed thread
neighbors.text: Today a sister tied a rakhi, a thread of protection, on her brother's wrist. In Sri Lanka, Thailand and other Theravada Buddhist lands, monks chant protective verses called paritta while holding a white cotton thread. Afterward, pieces of the thread are tied around people's wrists, a reminder of the blessing and the teaching it carried.
neighbors.difference: A rakhi binds two people: a sister's prayer and a brother's promise. The paritta thread carries the blessing of chanted teachings, and Buddhist teachers say its real protection is a mind shaped by those words.
neighbors.shared: a light thread on the wrist can carry a heavy promise.
neighbors.sources: paritta chanting and the blessed thread (described) · Karaniya Metta Sutta, Sutta Nipata 1.8, often among the verses chanted

neighbors.heading: worn close
neighbors.text: Today a thin thread on a wrist carried a promise of protection. Some Catholics wear something small too: a scapular, two little squares of brown cloth on cords, or a blessed medal, as a sign of belonging to Mary and trusting her care. The Church calls these sacramentals: blessed signs that dispose a person to receive God's grace.
neighbors.difference: A rakhi is a bond between siblings, a brother pledging to stand by his sister. A scapular binds the wearer to Mary and to God, and the Church teaches it is no charm; it means something only with faith and prayer.
neighbors.shared: a small thing worn close can remind you you're not alone.

neighbors.heading: work keeps the body going
neighbors.text: Today Paul worked at a tentmaker's bench, paying his own way while he taught. Hindus hear a call to work in the Bhagavad Gita. Krishna tells Arjuna: do your work, for action is better than doing nothing; without action, even the body could not be kept going. (paraphrase) A day's honest labor, in that picture, is part of the path.
neighbors.difference: Paul chose a trade so he could teach about Christ without charge. In the Gita, work is Arjuna's own duty, done without clinging to its results, and Krishna speaks there as God.
neighbors.shared: honest work with your hands can be part of the path.

neighbors.heading: a trade and the teaching
neighbors.text: Today Paul worked at a bench all week, then went to the synagogue on the sabbath. The rabbis prized that pairing. In Pirkei Avot, Rabban Gamliel says the study of Torah is best joined to a trade, because the effort of both keeps wrongdoing out of mind. (paraphrase) Another teacher there says it in two words: love work. (paraphrase)
neighbors.difference: Paul worked so he could teach about Christ free of charge, by his own choice. In Pirkei Avot, a trade beside Torah study is a way of life for anyone, and the teaching is the Torah itself.
neighbors.shared: the hands that work and the mind that learns belong together.

neighbors.heading: whatsoever ye do
neighbors.text: Today Krishna asked that whatever you do, eat or give be laid down as an offering. Christians know a line with the same reach. Paul writes to the church at Corinth: "Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God." The ordinary verbs of a day come first in his list too.
neighbors.difference: In the Gita, Krishna speaks as God and accepts even a leaf offered in love. Paul writes to Christians, who give glory to God through Jesus Christ, whom they call Lord.
neighbors.shared: an ordinary day can be handed over, one task at a time.

neighbors.heading: my living and my dying
